docs.title: evaluator workshop: Does your evaluator deserve your trust?
docs.text: This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Build a repeatable evaluator for the path you changed in M1 (LO6). Explain what it measures, demonstrate a defect it catches, and distinguish agreement with an anchor set from evidence of general correctness. This workshop and M2 use the same ci-dashboard repository, calibration report and local-gate evidence.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Follow Week 0 setup to check that you can run the practices, and for model access, the launcher and its profile resolver. Use the supplied evaluator kit, one short feature specification, and the ci-dashboard adapter fixture. All examples below start at the reviewed course root. Replace VERSION and DIGEST with resolver output; they are placeholders, not additional model settings.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Specify the question (30 minutes). Take the path you changed in M1 and state the task, environment, agent/implementation and scorer in fourtuple.json, following the schema. Describe one failure your evaluator should reject and one limitation. Start with the independent fixture adapter below, then reuse its structure for your path; do not rebuild the framework.

  2. Generate, then test (60 minutes). Create an isolated public workspace:

sh mkdir evaluator-work cp capstone/evaluator-workshop/student/anchor-cases.json capstone/evaluator-workshop/student/evaluator.py capstone/evaluator-workshop/student/judge.py capstone/evaluator-workshop/student/verify.py capstone/evaluator-workshop/student/prompt.txt evaluator-work/ cp evals/evaluator-kit/calibrate.py evals/evaluator-kit/calibration-policy.yaml evaluator-work/

Edit evaluator.py: evaluate(builds, observed) must return a Boolean indicating whether the observed result satisfies the imported ci-dashboard build summary under the fixture specification. In cases.json, write up to thirty distinct [builds, expected] assertions. Ten valid cases reach the automatic case ceiling; extra valid cases cannot reduce it. Generate or write your candidate, then run the supplied assertions:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace evaluator-work -- python verify.py

The starter returns False, so its first assertion fails. Diagnose that failure, fix the ordinary case, then check a passing main branch, a failing or canceled main build, a feature-only summary and malformed input. observed must be a real Boolean: do not coerce 1, "true", 0 or null into a passing result. Extra record fields are ignored by the fixture after branch and status have been validated; status matching is case-sensitive, and duplicate main records are each checked. Keep verify.py unchanged for the supplied local smoke gate; put your own additional examples in cases.json. A hardcoded list passing this public smoke is insufficient: the teacher challenges the evaluator on other inputs with an independent oracle. For your M1 path, implement the same separation: implementation output crosses into the scorer as data; acceptance truth stays outside the implementation process.

  1. Label and freeze (75 minutes). Open the supplied anchor-cases.json, which contains exactly thirty synthetic id/input records. Label every case independently before viewing model judgments. The teaching team keeps its item-level anchor labels privately and runs the one permitted comparison against your exact human.json bytes before collecting any judge output. You receive only an aggregate result (agreement, kappa, confusion matrix and Unknown rate), never an answer for an item. Save an array of records with the four fields id, input, label and reason. The IDs and inputs must match anchor-cases.json exactly; do not invent cases. Human labels are Pass or Fail, with a reason. Submit the labels through the approved course channel once. Keep the returned aggregate comparison with your M2 evidence; it is not a per-case answer key. Freeze the supplied seed-308 split before prompt tuning:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace evaluator-work --output evaluator-freeze-01 -- python calibrate.py freeze --human human.json --out split.json cp evaluator-freeze-01/split.json evaluator-work/split.json

The manifest records twenty development IDs, ten holdout IDs and a data hash. Have the teaching team retain this exact manifest through the existing assignment channel before tuning; keep its acknowledgment with your existing M2 evidence. The teacher binds the comparison to split.json.human_sha256 and requires the documented anchor agreement floor before judge collection. A hash that you can rewrite does not prove the holdout was held aside. No extra disclosure form is required. Do not feed human labels to the judge.

  1. Calibrate and revise (75 minutes). Start with only the twenty development IDs listed in the retained split.json. In a separate judge workspace, make inputs.json containing their IDs and input text only, with no human labels or reasons. The supplied judge.py sends five rows per bounded request and accepts this shorter array. Use the kit's local-recording command or an authenticated recording for those exact inputs and prompt. Inspect development judgments only, discuss one error, get workshop feedback and revise prompt.txt once. Retain Unknown and all attempt records, including failures.

Freeze the final prompt with the teacher before requesting or viewing holdout judgments. Collect the ten untouched holdout inputs once with that prompt. Also collect the twenty development inputs with the same final prompt, or reuse their existing authenticated records if the prompt has not changed. Assemble the thirty final rows in judge.json, preserving ID, input, label and reason. The teacher retains the final prompt and original recording provenance; do not mix prompt revisions.

Only now run the full report, which requires all thirty rows and reveals both partitions. Do not use it for development tuning:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace evaluator-work --output evaluator-report-01 -- python calibrate.py report --human human.json --judge judge.json --manifest split.json --prompt prompt.txt --out report.json cp evaluator-report-01/report.json evaluator-work/report.json

Read agreement, Cohen's kappa, confusion matrix, Unknown rate and disagreement IDs. Explain the development error, your revision and the actual holdout result even if it misses a band. After viewing holdout errors, keep this result; any further tuning requires a new teacher-frozen set for another confirmatory evaluation. Ordinary checks replay authenticated frozen records through course_llm FAKE. FAKE checks the pipeline, not real-model behavior or human annotation quality.

  1. Run the smoke gate and pin your regressions (30 minutes). Copy the supplied local gate into the M2 workspace, make it executable, and run it from the course root:

sh cp evals/evaluator-kit/run-regression.sh evaluator-work/run-regression.sh chmod +x evaluator-work/run-regression.sh evaluator-work/run-regression.sh --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \ --workspace evaluator-work

The script is a fixed smoke gate. It copies only evaluator.py and verify.py into a temporary workspace and runs the four unchanged assertions in verify.py through the course launcher. A failing candidate returns a non-zero status; fix it and rerun the same command until it passes. The script never reads cases.json or any other case file, so it cannot notice a deleted case. Keep your path's must-reject regressions in a regression file of your own beside your path's evaluator in your project repository. Write the expected number of cases in that file as a constant and check it against the number that ran, so that deleting a case makes the file fail. Keep the file out of this workshop's snapshot folder, which holds only the files listed under Deliverables. Show how each assertion relates to the spec. This is M2 feedback; it does not require a course-provided runner.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Submit one M2/evaluator workshop snapshot: anchor-cases.json, fourtuple.json, evaluator.py, cases.json, verify.py, judge.py, prompt.txt, human.json, judge.json, split.json, report.json, run-regression.sh, and your existing README.en.md explanation. The two calibration helpers may be included unchanged. Export files without .git, caches, symlinks or teacher assets. Reference the teacher's retained split/recording acknowledgment; do not put their receipt storage inside your submitted workspace.

Keep only the prompt versions, required judge outputs, disagreement analysis and relevant launcher/local-gate results. Do not export unrelated conversations. Explain what passed, what failed and what the holdout result can support. Write a short unaided reflection on a prediction error and the verification that changed your mind.

Use this note once, with the same evidence ID in M2: “Evidence ID: ...; AI use: none, or actual tool/model and purpose; my verification: ...; artifact/result references: ...”. Refer to your existing M2 work record.

docs.title: Feedback and M2
docs.text: Reuse this individual practice in M2, with feedback and one revision before the technical freeze. The 100-point diagnostic measures evaluator behavior and provides feedback; evaluator workshop has no separate weighted course mark. Keep the same annotations, evaluator and local-gate evidence in M2, including actual annotation and judge provenance.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Automatic points: fourtuple schema 10; up to ten independently valid executable cases 20; evaluator challenge correctness 15; recomputed calibration 30; supplied runnable CI smoke gate 5. The public policy awards calibration 30/20/10 when holdout kappa is at least 0.8/0.4/0.0 and Unknown rate is at most 0.1/0.2/0.3 respectively; otherwise zero. Boundaries are inclusive. Undefined kappa earns no band. The teacher-retained anchor comparison must also reach the policy's 0.95 agreement floor; a copied judge record cannot satisfy that gate. These are course grading choices, not industry reliability claims.

Twenty points await human review: feature evaluation design 10 and annotation/provenance quality 10, using the course specification and human-verification rubric dimensions. The reviewer checks all labels, split timing, holdout independence and your error analysis. Synthetic example labels do not establish that you performed manual labeling. Pending human items have no assigned score. Local feedback is not a formal grade; formal scoring uses the course's trusted grading and human-review process.

Allowed scaffolding and optional extensions do not reduce the attainable score. Your evaluator artifact is part of M2; the individual defense checks your evaluation understanding. Weekly self-checks give formative feedback. A failed calibration band calls for honest analysis, not changing the report.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Green for code, test and prompt development. Human annotations and unaided reflections must be written by people. Never use the judge's answers as the human reference labels. Use synthetic or authorized de-identified examples and omit credentials and personal data.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Five hours, including the workshop, verification and explanation. The teaching team prepares the private anchor labels and runs one comparison per student; that comparison is not an extra project assignment. At the first hour, seek help if the ordinary fixture case still fails; at three hours, seek help if the split or replay cannot run. Use the supplied adapters and keep one path. The time box is a help checkpoint, not an automatic stop or penalty.

docs.title: Local incident drill
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This is a small, deterministic M2 recovery exercise for the single ci-dashboard project. It uses synthetic JSON state files and writes only to a run directory chosen for this exercise. It does not start the application, contact a hosted service, open a socket, resolve DNS, read environment variables or execute a student runbook.

docs.title: Before the drill
docs.text: The drill scripts and templates are in this folder. The teaching team hands out the rest in class: a frozen snapshot of synthetic ci-dashboard state and one scenario. The scenario stays with the teaching team until the drill starts, because its fault and recovery values are what you diagnose. Until you have them, the commands below will not run; practise with observe before you repair instead.

docs.title: Run the drill
docs.text:
Save the snapshot in capstone/incident-drill/instructor/ and the scenario in capstone/incident-drill/instructor/scenarios/; drill.py looks for the scenario there by name. Then, from the course root, use a fresh run directory and the seed you were given:

mkdir -p capstone/incident-drill/instructor/scenarios /tmp/ase-incident-demo
python3 capstone/incident-drill/drill.py \
  --snapshot capstone/incident-drill/instructor/snapshot-ci-dashboard.json \
  --scenario status-cache-outage \
  --seed <your seed> \
  --run-dir /tmp/ase-incident-demo

The command records baseline.json, the injected current.json and state.json. A second invocation with the same snapshot, scenario, seed and run directory is idempotent; it returns the existing evidence without injecting a second fault. Inspect the changed synthetic status before attempting recovery.

Complete your copy of runbook.template.md, then run:

python3 capstone/incident-drill/recover.py \
  --run-dir /tmp/ase-incident-demo \
  --runbook path/to/student-runbook.md

Recovery validates the runbook headings, records its hash, restores the synthetic baseline, and checks that the resulting state has the original digest. It never evaluates or executes Markdown or shell text. Repeating the recovery command after a successful verification is also idempotent. Delete the temporary run directory after the teaching team has copied the minimal evidence required by the M2 work record.

docs.title: Safety and evidence
docs.text:
The scripts are intentionally smaller than a deployment system. They model the diagnosis, recovery and verification decisions without pretending to prove container isolation. Do not run them with a real deployment manifest, real credentials, participant material or a path that is a symlink. A malformed snapshot, scenario mismatch, changed baseline or modified injected state fails closed. A student record should include the snapshot, scenario, seed, observed fault, stop condition, recovery digest and remaining uncertainty. The postmortem.en.md template keeps this in the same work record; it is not a second assessment submission.

Use the drill only for the local, synthetic exercise described above.

docs.title: The 60-minute session
docs.text: The session uses 10 minutes to state the expected user-visible invariant and write a prediction, 15 to run and inspect the injected state, 15 to compare one observation with the runbook, 10 to recover and verify, and 10 to write the short postmortem. Each student runs the same local scenario with a distinct seed and writes their own diagnosis and verification. If a local safety precondition fails, stop and record the failure category; use the supplied synthetic walkthrough or an approved accessible equivalent rather than running on a host deployment.

docs.title: Local incident postmortem
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This template records one synthetic, loopback-free incident drill. Keep it with the same run directory evidence and remove any personal or credential material before submission.

  • Incident ID:
  • Snapshot / scenario / seed:
  • Observed impact:
  • First distinguishing evidence:
  • Recovery decision and stop condition:
  • Verification evidence:
  • What remained uncertain:
  • One prevention or monitoring change:
  • Student evidence ID:

docs.title: One repository, one verified path
docs.text: This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: enter your ci-dashboard repository in weeks 3–4 and agree one small change.
  • Hand in: one M0 PR linking your context and discovery evidence, specification, acceptance checks and work record.
  • Done when: each M0 criterion in the public rubric has a revision, evidence link and observed result or an explicit missing observation.
  • Time box: reuse the context and discovery workshops' estimates and record predicted and actual time in the existing work record; this entry adds no separate workshop.

Enter the supplied ci-dashboard student package in week 3. Do not copy instructor files or the complete private checkout into a work area. Use the Week 0 route for execution.

docs.title: Start the project and submit M0
docs.text: Keep one ci-dashboard repository for the whole capstone. The steps below are the complete M0 entry path; the context and discovery workshops add evidence to this same work, not a second submission.

docs.title: 1. Get the student repository
docs.text:
1. Finish the Week 0 setup, including the launcher check. Ask the teaching team for the public ci-dashboard student package and create one personal repository from that package. Do not clone or copy the course checkout, instructor directory, hidden tests, answer keys or allocation files.
  2. Record the starting commit in your work record. Keep the supplied launcher and public fixtures unchanged until you have run the baseline smoke check:

sh python3 -I launch.py smoke

This is the application's safety launcher; follow the supplied application start guide. A smoke pass only establishes the baseline; it is not acceptance evidence for your change.

docs.title: 2. Run the offline check and use the shared PR explanation
docs.text:
Run python3 -I launch.py smoke for each candidate revision in the supplied launcher environment. Keep the revision and output in your work record. This is an offline smoke check, not a model call or acceptance of your change; do not replace the launcher with commands that run the application on the host. If the smoke check fails, preserve the failure and explain the next verification step in the work record.

For each pull request, copy the body from the course PR template and keep its ## Explain gate section. The four question headings must remain unchanged: what changed, why, which inputs are most likely to fail, and what you personally verified. Read the explain-gate guide before the first PR. Its structural check is feedback about the shape of the explanation only. It does not score, review or approve the change. To review the current revision, ask the approved model for a bounded review of the diff in a fresh context. Then mark each finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with your own evidence and record the result. If model review is unavailable, ask a TA. The TA checks your M1 evidence. Reuse the same PR explanation and evidence ID in your work record instead of opening a separate explanation report.

docs.title: 3. Keep the evidence record in the repository
docs.text:
Use these stable locations so a reviewer and marker can follow one link from the submitted revision:

  • The workshop's public paths (including interviews/index.yaml and spec/feature.en.md) contain the two discovery records and specification. docs/m0/ may hold the context-workshop trace and comparison, the boundary check, the skill trigger test, the tested MCP tool-server result, and the executable acceptance checks. Link each item to the commit and command that produced it.
  • docs/work-record.md is one copy of the work-record template carried through M0–M4. For M0 it links the discovery observations, assumptions, frozen scope, acceptance cases and the verification result. Keep one evidence ID per criterion and put the single AI-use note for the work in this record.

Use the discovery workshop's two supplied synthetic personas for the first run. For live activities, submit only the workshop's de-identified evidence and teacher-checked consent/purpose reference; keep raw or identifying material in the approved private location. All participant material, including de-identified derivatives, stays out of model prompts. Write discovery notes and personal explanations yourself. A classroom rehearsal is not a participant session.

docs.title: 4. Complete and hand in M0
docs.text:
Use the two discovery activities and the context workshop on the same repository. Before changing the code, write your predictions and observations, separate observations from assumptions, and freeze one small need with its constraints. Then write one executable specification and acceptance check for that need. It must cover a normal input, a boundary input and a failure input, each with an expected result.

Your M0 pull request and work record are ready when they link:

  1. both discovery records and the frozen need;
  2. the context trace, two fixed-budget context packets, permission-boundary result, skill trigger test and MCP tool-server protocol result;
  3. the normal, boundary and failure acceptance checks, independent expected results and observed output or explicit missing execution; and
  4. the agreed change, its revision, the verification command, a short explanation and your evidence ID.

The public M0–M4 rubric is the marking reference. M0 is 2 points. Its full, partial and zero-credit boundaries are defined only by that public rubric. Hand in this single M0 record through the course's published submission route, then carry the same repository into M1.

The discovery student guide supplies the smoke execution route. Check any additional acceptance tests against the specification yourself, or with a TA, and label them not executed until a reviewed test action is supplied. Do not replace their missing execution with the warm-up's result or a smoke pass. In the root README.md, link the M0 work record and its evidence ID; follow the GitHub submission guide using the announced M0 assignment ID and branch. Record the full submitted commit SHA, PR link, check result and unresolved observations in that same work record.

docs.title: Work to carry forward
docs.text:
The project is worth 20 points. M0 (2 points) combines the context and discovery/specification workshops with one agreed small change and its executable specification. M1 (6) combines the reviewed change with the testing and security workshops, an AGENTS.md for the repository, one hook gate, and an agent-readiness scorecard taken at the start and end of M1 with one blocker removed between them. M2 (6) combines the evaluator, deployment preview and actual local incident evidence for the same path. M3 (3) starts when you submit a frozen snapshot tag: the teaching team runs the model audit, and you verify each finding as confirmed, refuted or undetermined and check one place yourself. M4 (3) records the response, user-informed iteration and expo demonstration.

The complete feature is not built here: you build it upstream in your C2 contribution; see the open-source contributions guide. One small change carried through M0–M4 can reach the highest band. Extra features and additional integrations do not increase the full-mark threshold. Workshop evidence stays in its corresponding milestone rather than becoming a second submission. Carry the product forward; one evidence ID supports one criterion. Repeating a reference does not earn extra points. The work record provides a short structure.

Read the public M0–M4 rubric for full, partial and zero-credit boundaries; it is the marking reference, and this kit does not create a second score or submission. Start M1 from the reliable-change instructions.

docs.title: M2 evidence
docs.text:
M2 combines the evaluator for the path you changed in M1, a local deployment preview, and a recovery record. Keep the evidence on the same ci-dashboard work and cite the commit that produced it. Submit:

  1. A short deployment note showing the exact command, the loopback address, the fixed synthetic-data seed, and the observed /healthz and /readyz responses.
  2. The evaluator command and its result, including the input, expected outcome, and observed outcome for the path's important case.
  3. A recovery record from the local incident exercise: request ID, relevant structured log lines, the failure observation, the repair, and a successful health/readiness check after recovery. Do not include passwords, API keys, personal data, or raw user content.

The supplied preview helper is documented in capstone/kit/deployment/README.en.md. Do not run it on your own machine: the teaching team runs it on your frozen revision, and you record the output it gives you. init-db initializes the local baseline and sample --seed records deterministic synthetic evidence.

docs.title: Acceptance and iteration
docs.text:
Before asking an agent to change code, agree a smallest useful behavior and an independent expected result. Preserve a failing regression, inspect a bounded diff and verify affected callers. Decide whether to accept, narrow, obtain one missing observation or stop. Security fixes also need positive tests for allowed behavior.

Use two discovery activities of your own for M0 and three usability sessions spread across weeks 11-13. Consent, minimal data and approved equivalent participation follow the course policies. A classroom rehearsal is not a real participant session. A recorded demonstration is a labeled fallback, not new execution evidence. Keep the discovery work, specification, and verification in your ci-dashboard repository; it is not a second submission.

Explain requirements, evaluation, security and operation in your individual defense. A project demo cannot replace your own explanation.

docs.title: Agent-readiness scorecard
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

An agent can change a repository safely only if it can find the change point, read the rules, run fast and repeatable tests, and hit the same checks your project requires. This scorecard turns that readiness into observations. The repository and numbers in the worked example below are course-made for teaching.

You score ci-dashboard twice during M1:

  • Start: in week 5, before your first reviewed change merges. Record the commit you scored.
  • End: when you submit M1, on the M1 head commit.

The change between the two scorecards, plus one blocker you removed and measured again, is your M1 modernisation evidence. Put both scorecards in your M1 work record. This is not a new submission or mark.

Run every command through the course launcher described in Week 0 setup.

docs.title: Score one dimension
docs.text:
1. Generate. You may ask an approved agent to propose a level and evidence for a dimension. Treat the answer as a list of claims, not a score.
  2. Choose a disproving observation. For each claim, decide which output or file would show it is false. For example, "tests are fast" is disproved by the runner's time.
  3. Verify. Run the command or open the file at the scored commit. Record the commit, the exact command or path, and what you observed.
  4. Score. Give the highest level where you can show every anchor. A dimension with no evidence link is recorded as 1, whatever you believe about it.
  5. Name the top blocker. Write the single observation that keeps this dimension from the next level.

Score the repository as it is at the commit, not as you plan to make it.

The student ci-dashboard package starts without a test suite or merge gates, so a level-1 start on Tests or Checks is expected. python3 -I launch.py smoke is a runnable smoke-test command and may be recorded as such, but it does not by itself provide a test suite or a merge gate.

docs.title: The four dimensions
docs.text: Each level includes everything in the levels below it.

docs.title: Structure: can an agent find the change point?
docs.text:
Probe: pick one behaviour your M0 feature touches. Starting from the README and file names, predict the function an agent must change. Then open files until you reach it and record each file you opened.

Level Observable anchor 1 No written map from behaviour to code. 2 A map exists (a README table or context file), but at least one level-3 anchor is not met, such as an entry you checked being wrong at the scored commit or the change point sitting in a function that mixes unrelated work such as routing, SQL and formatting. 3 Every map entry you checked is accurate, and the change point is in a function with one responsibility (no routing, SQL and formatting mixed). The probe reached the change point in three file opens or fewer. Each module's responsibility, and what it must not import or own, is written down. 4 A module boundary is enforced by a test or check, and you show it failing on a deliberate violation.

Evidence: the probe log (behaviour, files opened in order, path:line of the change point); for level 4, the failing output.

docs.title: Documentation: are the rules written where an agent reads them?
docs.text:
Probe: give a fresh agent session only the context file. Ask how to install, run and test the project, and what must never change. Then copy and run every command it gives you.

Level Observable anchor 1 No context file (such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md), or the file lists no run or test command. 2 A context file lists commands, but at least one fails when copied at the scored commit, or at least one level-3 anchor is not met, such as no project invariant (behaviour or security rule that must not change) being written down. 3 Every listed command runs as written through the launcher. At least three invariants are written down, and each names the test or check that protects it. 4 A check runs the documented commands, so a stale command fails the check. You show it failing once.

Evidence: the file path at the commit, the output of each documented command, and the invariant-to-test list.

docs.title: Tests: fast, repeatable, covering what you will change
docs.text:
Before measuring, agree a time budget for the test command you will run after every agent change. If you have no reason to choose otherwise, use 30 seconds as reported by the test runner. The launcher's own safety checks are not part of this time.

Probe: run the full test command twice at the scored commit and keep the runner's summary line both times. Search the tests for hidden inputs: the real clock, unseeded randomness, network access, test order and files outside the workspace. Then list the code paths your M1 change will touch. Break one on purpose, run the tests, record the result and revert.

Level Observable anchor 1 Both full-suite runs fail, or no runnable test command or test exercises the paths you will change. 2 At least one full-suite run passes, but at least one of these holds: it exceeds the time budget; a test reads a hidden input; the runs differ; or a deliberate break of a path you will change goes undetected. 3 Two passing runs with the same pass/fail result for every test, both within the budget, no hidden inputs, and the deliberate break makes a test fail. 4 Failure messages name the broken behaviour. Your testing workshop evidence shows each surviving mutant on the changed paths was killed or explained.

Evidence: both summary lines, the hidden-input search, and the deliberate-break output.

docs.title: Checks: what must an agent's change pass?
docs.text:
Probe: list every gate that runs before merge: formatting, lint, type check, secret scan, dependency audit, hooks and CI. Make two deliberately bad changes: add an unused import and add a project-defined canary such as PROJECT_CANARY_0123456789ABCDEF to a source file, with a custom scanner rule such as PROJECT_CANARY_[A-Z0-9]{16}. Record which gate stopped each change, then revert.

Level Observable anchor 1 No automatic gate. Correctness depends on someone remembering to run something. 2 An unused-import change can merge because gates can be run by hand, nothing requires them, or a gate already fails at the scored commit and is ignored. 3 One offline command or CI job runs every gate and exits non-zero when any gate fails; it stops an unused-import change. 4 The gates also run where the agent works, through a hook before a commit is offered, so the agent sees the failure itself. A secret scan is among them and its custom rule stops the project canary.

Evidence: the gate command, its failing output for each bad change it stopped, which gate (if any) let the canary pass, and its passing output after the revert.

docs.title: Worked example: "the tests are fast"
docs.text:
shelf-loans is a small library-loan service. Loans last 14 days, and the library is closed on Sundays. You score the Tests dimension at the start of the milestone.

# loans/policy.py
from datetime import date, timedelta


LOAN_DAYS = 14


def due_date(borrowed: date) -> date:
    due = borrowed + timedelta(days=LOAN_DAYS)
    if due.weekday() == 5:  # the library is closed on Sundays
        due += timedelta(days=1)
    return due

# tests/test_policy.py (one of 18 tests)
from datetime import date, datetime
import time

import pytest

from loans.policy import due_date


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def warm_cache():
    time.sleep(2)  # let the catalogue cache warm up


def test_due_date_is_not_sunday():
    today = datetime.now().date()
    assert due_date(today).weekday() != 6

The warm_cache fixture is in test_policy.py, so it covers all 18 tests in this example only if those tests are in that module. Moving it to conftest.py would broaden its scope.

Generation. You ask an agent to score the Tests dimension. It answers:

Tests: 4. The suite is fast and deterministic, and tests/test_policy.py covers the due-date rules.

Verification. The answer contains three claims: fast, deterministic and covering the due-date rules. You check each one at the scored commit.

Claim What you ran or opened Observation Holds? Fast The test command, twice 18 passed in 36.42s and 18 passed in 36.38s; budget 30 s. Each test spends 2 s in warm_cache, and no test reads that cache. No Deterministic Hidden-input search datetime.now() in test_due_date_is_not_sunday. Two passing runs on the same day cannot show what happens on another weekday. No Covers due-date rules Set LOAN_DAYS = 13, ran the tests, reverted 18 passed on a Wednesday. Nothing checks the loan length. No

Start score: Tests 2. The suite runs and passes, but it is over budget, it reads the clock, and a deliberate break goes undetected. Top blocker: the due-date test depends on the day it runs.

Removing the blocker. You remove the unused sleep and replace the clock with seven fixed dates, Monday 2 March to Sunday 8 March 2026:

from datetime import date, timedelta

import pytest

from loans.policy import due_date


WEEK = [date(2026, 3, 2) + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(7)]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("borrowed", WEEK, ids=str)
def test_due_date_is_two_weeks_later_or_next_open_day(borrowed):
    due = due_date(borrowed)
    assert due.weekday() != 6, f"due on a Sunday: {due}"
    assert (due - borrowed).days in (14, 15)

The first run reports 2 failed, 22 passed in 0.41s. Loans borrowed on 7 and 8 March are due on Sunday 22 March. The old test only ever checked the day it ran, so it passed on every run from Monday to Friday. The code compares with Saturday (5) instead of Sunday (6). You record this defect and fix it in a separate reviewed change with this test as its regression.

End score: Tests 3. Two runs report 24 passed in 0.39s and 24 passed in 0.40s, no test reads a hidden input, and LOAN_DAYS = 13 now gives 6 failed, 18 passed. It is not 4 yet because you have no mutation evidence for this path.

The scorecard entry for this dimension:

Dimension Start (commit) End (commit) Evidence Blocker removed Tests 2 (a1b2c3d) 3 (e4f5a6b) Summary lines, hidden-input search and the LOAN_DAYS = 13 output at both commits Clock-dependent due-date test: replaced by seven fixed dates; before and after output linked

Use the same pattern of claim, disproving observation and recorded output for the other three dimensions.

docs.title: Worked example on ci-dashboard: Documentation and Checks
docs.text: The Week 5 worked example removes one blocker in each of the two dimensions a context file and a hook can raise today on ci-dashboard; Tests waits for a test command. It adds a context file with run and test commands and three invariants, each mapped to a check, and verifies the file with the fresh-session probe. It then adds a pre-commit hook that runs lint and stops an unused-import change. It shows the failing case, the passing case and the resulting scorecard rows.

docs.title: What to submit in M1
docs.text:
Add these to the M1 work record:

  1. Both scorecards: a level, commit and evidence link for each of the four dimensions, plus the top blocker named at the start.
  2. One removed blocker: the start observation, the reviewed change that removed it, and the same observation repeated at the end commit.
  3. One sentence per dimension explaining why the level changed or stayed the same.

docs.title: How it is marked
docs.text:
The scorecard is evidence for the agent workflow design dimension of the course rubric within M1's 6 points. Its four workflow levels are: context and configuration absent; context and configuration present without a gate or cost record; context, skills, hooks, permissions and evaluation gates with a cost record; and A/B or cost comparison plus reusable project norms.

  • Markers reopen a sample of your evidence links at the commits you name. A level that the evidence does not support is corrected to the level the evidence shows.
  • The size of the change does not earn marks. A dimension that honestly stays at 2 is acceptable. Scoring the start low to make the change look larger does not help, because start evidence is checked against the start commit.
  • One removed blocker with before-and-after observations is enough for full marks on this scorecard's M1 evidence. Removing more blockers does not raise this scorecard's ceiling.
  • Deleting or skipping tests, or turning off a gate, does not count as removing a blocker. It lowers the Tests or Checks level. Replacing a test with one that still fails on every deliberate break the old test caught is not deletion, as in the worked example. Markers check this by:
  • Re-running the intentional break recorded at the start on the end commit.
  • Comparing the passed, skipped, xfailed, and deselected counts in both summaries.
  • Reading the complete git diff <start> <end> -- <test paths> for the test paths.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Accepting an agent's level because it sounds right. Every level needs a command output or a file path at a named commit.
  • Treating two passing runs as proof of repeatability. Search the test code for hidden inputs as well.
  • Counting a gate that exists but does not block a bad change.
  • Timing the whole launcher command. Use the time the test runner reports.
  • Scoring planned work. Score what the commit shows, and put the plan in the blocker line.

docs.title: AI use
docs.text: You may use an approved agent to propose levels and evidence. The verification commands, recorded observations and per-dimension explanations are your own. Note AI use once in the M1 work record and reuse its ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: About 45 minutes for each scoring pass. The first 15 minutes of the start pass are the Week 5 workshop's readiness activity. Removing the blocker is part of your M1 change, not extra work.

docs.title: Open-source contributions
docs.text:
Make four contributions across two repositories, worth 30 marks in total. In each repository, start with a small onboarding fix, then make a substantive change. Move to the second repository after contribution 2. You practise entering unfamiliar codebases, verifying changes, and following their contribution rules (LO4, LO5, LO7, LO9).

Contribution Due Repository Scope Marks 1 Week 4 First Small, complete onboarding fix 5 2 Week 8 First Substantive change 10 3 Week 9 Second Small, complete onboarding fix 5 4 Week 12 Second Substantive change 10

Deadlines are Sunday at 23:59 in the due week. A small fix might repair a defect, test or documentation example. A substantive change solves a larger problem with a bounded scope and verifiable acceptance cases. Read the repository's rules before proposing work.

docs.title: Find a repository and submit your preferences
docs.text:
In week 2, rank your preferences on the volunteer form. The teaching team assigns the first repository and arranges the move to a different repository after contribution 2. At most five students work on a repository at one time.

The list prioritizes public open-source projects maintained or used by partners, with other active projects added. Every listed repository needs an OSI-approved licence, contribution guidelines, an AI-use policy that permits the planned work, and no CLA that assigns copyright. You may propose another repository for approval against these conditions. Do not start counted work there before approval.

The teaching team checks these conditions, records whether there is a partner maintainer contact, and publishes the list and allocation instructions. Contacts are not invented: the list records only people who have actually agreed to act as contacts.

Where to find or send things Publication or action Approved repositories and contribution-guide links The teaching team publishes the approved public repository list before Week 2. Partner maintainer contact for each repository, or no contact The teaching team confirms each partner maintainer contact, or records that there is none, before Week 2. Week 2 preferences and volunteering The teaching team publishes the volunteer form and allocation channel before Week 2 preferences are due. A repository or issue you propose; a scope change The teaching team publishes the approval channel before students propose a repository, issue or scope change. Four submissions and requests for TA acceptance review The teaching team publishes the submission channel and TA review-request route before the first contribution deadline. Pseudonymous account or course-hosted equivalent The teaching team publishes the private identity and equivalent-route channel before the first contribution is submitted.

Do not make a marked contribution to a repository owned by your own residency employer. Tell the teaching team privately if an allocation would cross that boundary so it can assign a different repository.

docs.title: Make and verify each change
docs.text:
1. Read and discuss. Read the licence, contribution guide, AI rules and relevant issue. Follow the project's process for agreeing the scope before starting unwanted work.
  2. Reproduce. Record the starting revision and a check that fails for the issue you intend to fix. For documentation, use an executable example or a repeatable check of the documented behaviour. Agree an appropriate check with a TA if necessary.
  3. Generate and inspect. Use the permitted assistance to make a small change. Inspect the diff and affected callers yourself; do not submit unexamined generated output.
  4. Verify. Run the check again and the relevant existing tests. Preserve the result that fails before the change and passes after it, with revisions and commands.
  5. Submit and respond. Follow the upstream PR, sign-off and disclosure process. Respond to review, verify revisions, and record what you changed or why the evidence supports retaining a decision.

For each contribution submit the issue and PR links, the submitted revision, the before and after verification results, and a brief explanation answering these four questions:

  • What changed?
  • Why was that change needed?
  • Which inputs or conditions could break it?
  • What did you personally verify?

Add one AI-use note to the existing work record, reused by ID, or state that no AI was used. Submit the project's required artifacts and these evidence links through the course submission channel; no general conversation export or separate disclosure file is required.

docs.title: Completion and quality
docs.text:
For a repository with a partner contact, a merged PR satisfies the completion condition. If the repository has no contact, or the maintainer has not replied within seven days, a TA instead makes an acceptance review against that project's contribution guidelines. Request that review with the PR, its contribution-guide link, and the dated request or discussion showing the lack of reply. Respond to the TA's findings as you would to upstream review. Your mark does not depend on the maintainer replying.

Completion does not remove the quality requirement. Low-quality AI-generated output earns zero marks, as judged by the maintainer or TA. Each contribution needs the failing and passing verification pair and your own answers above. Neither a merge alone nor a polished explanation replaces that evidence. If the issue becomes infeasible or its rules change, tell the teaching team before continuing and agree a new scope.

docs.title: Boundaries and rights
docs.text:
• Public upstream only: external contributions go only to public repositories. Residency, employer and partner-internal code never enters the course or a model.
  • Follow the project's AI rules: disclose assistance as it requires. If it disallows your planned use, change the workflow or repository; do not conceal AI use.
  • Identity: use a pseudonym where the project permits it. The teaching team keeps the account-to-student mapping privately. Check what names and email addresses a sign-off or agreement would expose before signing.
  • Copyright: you are never required to sign a CLA that assigns copyright. A CLA granting a non-exclusive licence is your choice after reading it.
  • Equivalent route: if you do not want to publish publicly or sign a CLA or DCO, you may choose the course-hosted equivalent without giving a reason. Tell the teaching team before publishing or signing. It supplies non-public practice repositories for the same four contributions, small then substantial in each of two repositories, with a TA acceptance review, the same rubric and the same maximum marks.
  • Keep private material private: do not send participant material, credentials, teacher files or another student's unpublished work to a model or upstream. Follow the project's private reporting process for a security problem and tell the teaching team; course attack payloads and seeded defects never go upstream.

These contributions are separate from the term project. The syllabus defines their marks and rules.

docs.title: Deployment preview
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This preview is for the ci-dashboard application only. It is a teaching aid, not a release or hosting command. It binds to 127.0.0.1, runs the existing deterministic init-db action, records the sample --seed output as evidence, and keeps its process state and generated sample under the application's ignored data/ directory.

docs.title: Where the preview runs
docs.text:
Do not run preview.py or manage.py on your own machine. The preview starts the application as an ordinary process, outside any sandbox, so every changed or model-written line in your revision would run with your account's access. On your own machine, run your revision only through the course launcher routes, such as the launch.py actions in the application start guide.

The preview never runs on a student machine. The teaching team runs it on the revision you freeze as your Week 10 technical snapshot, in an isolated environment that the teaching team chooses and announces. The same holds for any later preview of your revision, for example in user tests or the final demonstration.

docs.title: What you record
docs.text:
The teaching team gives you the preview's printed output and the request lines from its log. Keep these in your work record:

  1. The full commit SHA of the revision the preview ran, the exact command the teaching team ran, and its seed and count.
  2. The JSON line that up printed. up prints it only after both probes pass; it names the process, host, port, seed and count.
  3. The status result. status checks both /healthz and /readyz, reports each as health and ready, and exits non-zero when the process or either probe is unavailable. /healthz answers while the process serves requests; /readyz answers 503 until the database has its required tables.
  4. The request IDs and the few request lines you need to explain your M2 recovery observation.

The seeded sample is an evidence artifact; the application's initialized database remains the served baseline. down is safe to repeat and removes the transient state and sample files.

Each application response carries an X-Request-ID header. The application emits one JSON request record containing the request ID, method, path, status, and duration. The record deliberately excludes query values, form fields, cookies, authorization data, and response bodies. Preserve only the small set of lines needed to explain the M2 recovery observation.

M2 evidence includes the preview record above, the evaluator result, and the recovery check after the local incident exercise. The preview does not send network traffic, provision a hosted service, or provide a rollback or release approval.
