docs.title: What the comparison can and cannot show
docs.text:
The fixture is one function, so it cannot show every kind of blocker. The rows below are illustrative: they are the kinds of observation you will record in the studio on a whole repository, not results of the commands above.

Observation Supported claim Missing evidence The session found status_label in two file opens The map points to this change point for this revision Other behaviours may have different maps The documented check exits zero on the refactored copy These cases pass at this revision Callers, permissions and unlisted inputs The disordered copy has three test commands, two of which fail Documentation is a blocker for a fresh session Whether the implementation itself is correct A hook rejects an unused import with exit 2 The hook can stop that class of change Other checks and bypass paths

An agent may propose the score, but you choose it. For each dimension record the path or command, revision, observed result, the highest level whose anchors are all present, and one observation that would disprove the score.

docs.title: Four observable readiness dimensions
docs.text: Use levels 1–4. A level includes every lower-level anchor.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• 1: no map from a behaviour to its change point;
  • 2: a map exists, but a checked entry is wrong or mixes unrelated responsibilities;
  • 3: checked entries are accurate, the change point has one responsibility, and the probe reaches it in three file opens or fewer;
  • 4: a deliberate boundary violation fails a test or check.

Evidence is a behaviour, the files opened in order, a path:line change point and, at level 4, the failing result.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• 1: no context file or no runnable command;
  • 2: commands exist but one fails as written, or no invariant names the check that protects it;
  • 3: every listed command runs at the scored revision and at least three invariants name their checks;
  • 4: an automated check runs the documented commands and fails when one goes stale.

Evidence is the context-file path, each command and exit code, and the invariant-to-check list.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• 1: no runnable test exercises the change point;
  • 2: one run passes but a hidden input, nondeterminism or a deliberate break goes undetected;
  • 3: two repeatable runs agree, stay within the chosen budget, use no hidden input, and a deliberate break fails;
  • 4: failure messages identify the broken behaviour and mutation evidence accounts for surviving gaps.

Evidence is the two summaries, the hidden-input search, and the deliberate-break result.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• 1: no automatic gate;
  • 2: a gate can be run by hand but is not required, or it ignores an unused import;
  • 3: one offline command runs the required gates and exits non-zero for an unused import;
  • 4: the gate runs before a commit is offered and a secret canary is stopped by the project scanner.

Evidence is the gate command, failing and passing output, and the point where the gate is required.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Use the studio activity on your own project or contribution target repository. First freeze a baseline at a named commit. Give the agent only the files needed to answer one bounded question; inspect its proposal as untrusted text. Then run the repository's documented check and inspect the diff. If a command needs a credential, network access or an unknown install, stop and revise the boundary rather than running it.

Your first score is a four-row table with one evidence link and one disproving observation per row. Remove one blocker that is within your scope—for example, reconcile two test commands, add a map from a behaviour to its module, or make a check command deterministic. Run the same probe at the new commit and score again. A tidy directory without a changed observation does not raise a score.

Time-box the work: 15 minutes to choose the task and baseline, 25 minutes to score, 25 minutes to remove one blocker, 15 minutes to rerun the probes, and 10 minutes to write the decision. Ask for help at the first failed command; reserve the final ten minutes for revision.

docs.title: Supported execution
docs.text: Run the fixture commands on this page directly. Before running a project's own check, follow Tools and model access.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run the public fixture before and after reading the candidate:

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected  # expected: exit 1, 7 of 10 passed
python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py refactored  # expected: exit 0, 10 of 10 passed

For your repository, run the exact command it documents, record its exit code and inspect the changed-file list:

git status --short
git diff --check
git diff --name-only

A passing check is evidence for the inputs it covered. A score changes only when the observed anchor changes at a named revision. If the same command passes because its tests were deleted, its scope was weakened, or the agent supplied a result without a command, keep the old score and record the finding.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to detect it Correction Scoring from a polished README A listed command fails or names a missing file Run each command at the scored revision and lower the row until it passes Treating an agent's score as evidence No path, revision or output is attached Ask for one observable anchor and one disproof before recording a number Refactoring only for shorter code The candidate passes happy paths but loses normalization or a caller contract Add the distinguishing case, restore the invariant, and rerun the unchanged check Calling contradictory docs a test failure The same command is written three ways Choose one bounded source of truth and verify the chosen command, leaving the conflict recorded Running a generated command blindly It asks for a key, network or an unpinned install Stop, inspect the trust boundary, and run it only in a dedicated directory or container that holds no credentials; otherwise record the missing prerequisite Raising a score after deleting tests The test count or covered paths shrink Compare the old and new test lists and keep the score unchanged

End the work record with one decision: accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Name the evidence that supports it and the observation that would change it.

docs.title: Make your copy ready for an agent: a context file, a hook gate and a hand-off
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

The workshop's readiness activity scored one dimension of your ci-dashboard copy at its start commit. This practice removes the blockers that the worked example found in two dimensions, Documentation and Checks, this time on your own copy and at your own commits. You write an AGENTS.md, add one hook gate, split one task into hand-offs, and score again. Every part has a generation step and a verification step, and only the verification counts as evidence.

Time: about 80 minutes of M1 work, inside Week 5's published estimate: 25 minutes for the context file, 25 for the hook, 20 for the hand-off and 10 for the new score.

Route: everything below works offline with the course-written replays. A real agent session is optional and is used only where a part says so.

You need: your copy at the commit you scored in the workshop, the agent-readiness scorecard, the M1 description and the files in example/. Everything in example/ is course-written for teaching; none of it is a captured model response.

Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run each sh scripts/course-sandbox command from the course root, as Week 0 setup explains. Run launch.py commands from the root of your ci-dashboard copy. Create each workspace with your editor.

docs.title: Part 1: write an AGENTS.md and check that it changes something (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Generate. Write AGENTS.md at the root of your copy. You may start from agents-example.txt, or ask an agent to draft it from README.en.md, START.en.md, manage.py and your exploration notes. Either way, treat every line as a claim about your copy at this commit. Keep five short sections:

Section What it must say Run and test Every command a newcomer needs, exactly as it is typed, and the result that means it worked Before every commit The hook command from Part 2 and what its exit codes mean Invariants At least three rules that must not change, each naming the check that protects it Boundaries The files a feature change must not touch, and what a session must never do, such as install a package Report What a session hands back at the end: files changed, commands run with exit codes, and what it did not check

The whole file should fit on one screen. A rule that needs a paragraph to explain is a rule a session will half-follow. Keep the Run and test and Invariants sections short enough for the worked example's fresh-session probe, which refuses a section that does not fit in one launcher prompt.

Verify that every command runs. Copy each command from the file and run it as written, through the launcher it names. Write down the exit code and the first line of output. A smoke result from your exploration counts only if it is from the same commit. If a command fails as written, fix the line in the file and run it again; do not fix it in your head. Then run each invariant's check, including the deliberate violation, and restore the file afterwards with git restore.

Verify that the file changes what a session does. example/replay/ holds one bounded task given to two fresh sessions, one without the context file and one with it. The task, in handoff.json, is to add a skipped status to domains/labels.py. Each session's hand-back is in without.json and with.json, and what git diff --name-only printed afterwards is in without-diff.txt and with-diff.txt. Read both hand-backs and predict which one meets the hand-off.

Then check each one with check_handoff.py. It reads the hand-off, the hand-back and the diff, and never runs a command from them. Create week05-check in the course root and copy check_handoff.py and the five files from example/replay/ into it. Then run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json without.json without-diff.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json with.json with-diff.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json without.json

Expect exit_code 2 for the first command, with eight findings. The first is the session's list of changed files against the diff, which also contains pyproject.toml. The last is did not hand back 'not_checked' as a non-empty list. Expect exit_code 0 for the second command and PASS: the hand-back matches the hand-off; changed files taken from the diff. The third command checks the same hand-back without the diff. Its output no longer mentions pyproject.toml, because the checker can then compare only the session's own claims.

For each finding in the first run, name the line of the context file that removed it in the second run. The session without the file did reasonable things: it wanted a test, found no test command and installed one. It had no way to know that a dependency change is its own reviewed change. Then name what the file could not fix. The with session's exit codes are still its own claims until you open each launcher result, and its two not_checked items are now your next checks.

Optional, with an agent. On a scratch branch of your copy, give the same task to two fresh sessions of your approved agent, one with your AGENTS.md and one without it. Run any command a session proposes only through the launcher. Write each hand-back in the same JSON shape and check both with the commands above.

docs.title: Part 2: add one hook gate and make it fail (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Your Boundaries section says which files a feature change must not touch. A rule that only a session reads is a request. A hook that stops the commit is a gate.

Define the bad change first. Write down the event that the gate must stop: a commit whose changed files include a protected file. In the worked example, that is {"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py","pyproject.toml"]}. Write down the good event too, one your gate must let through: {"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py"]}.

Generate. Copy pre_commit.py into a new workspace, week05-gate. If your Boundaries list differs from the example's, give an agent the hook and your Boundaries section and ask it to change the protected set to match. Ask it not to read or run the files it checks. You can also make the edit yourself. Compare the result with the course hook's PROTECTED set and protected function, and read every changed line before you run it.

Verify: has it ever failed? A gate you have only seen pass has not been shown to stop anything. Copy labels_revised.py into the workspace as domains/labels.py. Predict each result, then run the bad event, the good event, and the bad event with the protected path spelled another way:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py","pyproject.toml"]}'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py"]}'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["./pyproject.toml"]}'

With the course hook, expect exit_code 2 and pyproject.toml: protected by AGENTS.md; change it in its own reviewed change for the first command. Expect exit_code 0 and PASS: no protected file and no unused import in 1 file(s) for the second. Expect exit_code 2 again for the third.

Read the reason, not only the exit code. A line that starts with REFUSED: means the hook rejected its input, and that is not your rule firing. A lint-only hook refuses pyproject.toml as "not an ordinary .py file": it exits 2, but for the wrong reason, and it would let launch.py through if the file were present. Your first run must print your rule's own line. Keep all three launcher results.

The hook runs two checks today: protected files, then lint. The test step waits for a test action in the project launcher; launch.py has no test action yet.

docs.title: Part 3: split one task into hand-offs (20 minutes)
docs.text:
A subagent is a fresh session with one role. It gets only the context that role needs and a hand-off: the task, the files it may change, the commands it may and must run, and what it hands back. Your AGENTS.md is the hand-off every session receives. A role's hand-off narrows it to one job. Here is a division of the skipped task:

Role Receives May change Runs Hands back Explorer The task and AGENTS.md Nothing Nothing; it only reads files callers: each path:line that calls status_label; open_questions Implementer The task, AGENTS.md and the explorer's callers domains/labels.py The hook and the smoke test changed, ran, not_checked Reviewer The task, the implementer's hand-off, the diff and the implementer's hand-back Nothing Nothing findings: each with a path:line and the check that would confirm it

The reviewer does not receive the explorer's notes or the implementer's reasoning. It judges the change against what was asked and what ran, not against a plan it has already read.

Generate. Choose your own first M1 change, or the skipped task if your change is not settled yet. Write three hand-offs in the shape of handoff.json, one per role. An explorer's or reviewer's hand-off has "may_change": [] and "run": []. Name the extra fields it hands back in hand_back, for example ["callers", "open_questions"]. You can ask an agent to draft them; you decide what each role may touch.

Act it out. Play each role yourself or give it to a fresh session. Do the implementer's work on a scratch branch, write its hand-back in the shape of with.json, and save what git diff --name-only prints as diff.txt. A read-only role's diff should be empty.

Verify. Create week05-roles and copy check_handoff.py into it, with each role's hand-off, hand-back and diff under names of your choice. Run the checker on each role as in Part 1, with your file names. Then do by hand what the checker cannot. Open each path:line the explorer returned. Rerun each check a reviewer finding names. Compare each ran entry with the launcher result you kept. A role that changed a file it was not given, or handed back nothing for a field, has broken the division. Narrow its hand-off and run it again.

In Week 6 you run a planner, an implementer and a reviewer as separate launcher runs on a real review task. This week's hand-offs are the contracts those runs need.

docs.title: Part 4: score again (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Score Documentation and Checks with the scorecard at the commit that adds your AGENTS.md and hook. Use the same probes as at the start and give the highest level where you can show every anchor.

Dimension Start End Evidence Blocker removed Documentation your start level The AGENTS.md path at the end commit, each command's result and each invariant's check Checks your start level The hook's failing and passing results, and the line in AGENTS.md that requires the hook before every commit

The worked example's file and hook reach 3 in both dimensions; your copy may score differently. The protected-file rule enforces a line of your Boundaries section, but it does not by itself move Checks: the scorecard's Checks anchors ask what stops an unused-import change and, at level 4, a secret scan that stops the canary. Write down what still keeps each dimension from level 4.

docs.title: What to keep
docs.text:
Put these in your existing M1 work record, linked by evidence ID:

  • the AGENTS.md commit and each command result from Part 1, plus your line-by-line answer for the replayed pair;
  • the hook's protected set, the three launcher results from Part 2 and the line in AGENTS.md that requires the hook;
  • your three hand-offs, the implementer's hand-back, diff.txt and the checker results;
  • both scorecard rows.

If an agent helped, add one AI-use note and reuse its ID. No transcript is needed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How you notice What to do The context file describes the plan, not the copy. A listed command fails when copied at the commit. Fix the line and run it again before scoring. The gate has only ever passed. You have no failing run that prints your rule's line. Run the bad event and keep the result. An exit 2 is counted as the rule firing. The output starts with REFUSED:. Fix the event or the workspace until your rule's line appears. A hand-back is taken at its word. No diff was given to the checker. Give it the git diff --name-only output; open the launcher results yourself. A reviewer gets the implementer's notes. The reviewer repeats the plan's reasoning. Hand it only the task, the hand-off, the diff and the hand-back.

docs.title: Week 5 reading paths
docs.text:
No external reading is required. The lesson uses the public, course-authored fixture and your own repository evidence. Read in this order:

  1. Notes, especially the four readiness dimensions and the comparison of disordered and prepared copies.
  2. The public starting function, then predict the cases in the verifier before opening the candidate files.
  3. Studio instructions, and the exact command your repository documents for its local check.
  4. Self-check, answering from paths and outputs rather than from an agent's confidence.

The fixture's command output is a reproducible teaching observation, not an industry statistic or a real model run. Do not cite a card or a README as a published source; name the file, revision, command and output that you actually checked.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Tie each conclusion to an anchor, a scored revision and an observation that another reader could repeat. These are sample reasoning paths, not a substitute for recording your own evidence.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: The missing Structure anchor is the map from a behaviour to its change point: four file opens without naming the caller also exceeds the three-open limit of level 3. A level-2 score claims that a map exists, so it is disproved if no file at the scored revision maps this behaviour to its caller and change point; the score is then 1.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: Level 2 is supported: commands exist, but two of the three fail as written. Record the one command that succeeds at the scored revision and its output. Running the listed alternatives at the same revision, then updating the README to match the successful path, would raise the evidence.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The distinguishing input is " PASS " (or another padded value): the rejected variant does not strip whitespace, while the refactored variant preserves input normalization. The fixed case list, including aliases and the unknown fallback, is the evidence.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The Tests anchor is unsupported because the date is uncontrolled. Supply a fixed date or inject a clock and run both test cases again at the scored revision.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Exit 2 establishes that the check rejected the unused import. It does not establish that other checks, a clean input or a complete check sequence succeeds; run those separately and record their commands and outputs.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Request the scored revision, exact command and path, observed output, and the reason the anchor level follows. A bare number cannot be reproduced or challenged.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: A caller test with " PASS " catches the regression because the shorter function returns unknown. Run the old and refactored implementations against the same fixed cases and keep the failing rejected result alongside the passing result.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Do not run that instruction with a real key or an unpinned installer. Use an isolated safe environment, replace the key with a placeholder, pin the dependency, and record the README path plus the command and output that can be reproduced without credentials.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Revisit the score downward or leave it unchanged until the six missing cases are explained. A smaller passing set does not prove improved readiness: compare the old and new test inventories and restore or justify every removed case.

docs.title: Retrieval prompts
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Record the case, the context paths and the scored revision, then rerun the same command.

Retrieval 2. A clean tree says nothing about a measurable limit or check; name both before increasing the score.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check
docs.text:
Answer in your existing work record, then compare with a peer or the public answer guidance and the notes. These prompts are preparation and carry no separate marks.

  1. You have opened four files and still cannot name the caller of a function. Which Structure anchor is missing, and what observation would disprove a level-2 score?
  2. A repository lists pytest, make test and python -m unittest, but only one works at the scored commit. Which Documentation level is supported, and what evidence would raise it?
  3. Why does python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected fail while the refactored variant passes? Name the input that distinguishes them.
  4. Two identical test runs pass, but the tests read the current date. Which Tests claim is unsupported, and what fixed input would remove the uncertainty?
  5. A hook exits 2 for an unused import. What does that establish about Checks, and what does it leave untested?
  6. An agent says “readiness 4” without a revision, command or path. What must you request before recording a score?
  7. The refactored code is shorter but a caller sends padded input. Which verification step catches the regression?
  8. A README asks you to paste a key into an environment variable and run an unpinned installer. What boundary applies, and what safe evidence can you collect instead?
  9. After removing one blocker, the test count falls from 24 to 18 and the remaining tests still pass. What should happen to the score and why?

docs.title: Retrieval prompts
docs.text:
R1. Retrieval 1. What recorded case, context paths and scored revision turn a generated proposal into a verified observation?

R2. Retrieval 2. Which measurable check and limit are missing when a readiness claim relies on a clean directory tree alone?

docs.title: Agent-ready codebases
docs.text:
Week 5 · Structure, documentation, tests and checks

A tidy tree is a hypothesis. Evidence decides.

docs.title: Today
docs.text:
• Give the same bounded task to a disordered and a prepared repository.
  • Find the blockers that make an agent guess.
  • Score four dimensions from observable anchors.
  • Remove one blocker and test whether the score changes.

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
Replace status conditionals with a lookup.

Preserve whitespace, case, aliases and the unknown fallback.

The proposal is text until a person inspects and verifies it.

docs.title: Two copies, one task
docs.text:
An illustrative contrast, not fixture output.

Disordered copy Prepared copy Three possible test commands One command at the scored revision Contradictory rules One named contract Check needs an unknown install Check runs locally Change point is hidden Map names the caller and module

docs.title: What the comparison proves
docs.text:
It shows which guesses the repository forces a fresh session to make.

It does not prove the implementation is correct, all callers are covered or every command is safe.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Ask for a bounded expression as text.

Inspect the diff and expected behavior.

python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py rejected
python lectures/week-05/fixture/verify.py refactored

docs.title: A rejected shortcut
docs.text:
LABELS.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

What disappeared?

strip() was part of the contract.

docs.title: The verified refactor
docs.text:
LABELS.get(raw.strip().lower(), "unknown")

The structure changed.

The behavior cases remain.

docs.title: Evidence is bounded
docs.text:
A passing fixture supports its listed inputs at one revision.

A caller map supports the paths you opened.

A hook failure supports the rule it actually enforced.

docs.title: Four dimensions
docs.text:
1. Structure
  2. Documentation
  3. Tests
  4. Checks

Each score is the highest level whose anchors you can show.

docs.title: Structure: find the change point
docs.text:
1 No map.

2 A map exists, but an entry is wrong or responsibilities mix.

3 Entries checked are accurate; the path reaches a single-responsibility change point in ≤3 opens.

4 A deliberate boundary violation fails a check.

docs.title: Documentation: write the rules
docs.text:
1 No context file or runnable command.

2 A listed command fails or invariants have no protecting checks.

3 Commands run at the scored revision; three invariants name checks.

4 An automated check catches a stale command.

docs.title: Tests: test the claim
docs.text:
1 No runnable test covers the change point.

2 A pass hides nondeterminism or a deliberate break.

3 Two repeatable runs agree and a deliberate break fails.

4 Failure messages and mutation evidence explain the remaining gaps.

docs.title: Checks: make failure visible
docs.text:
1 No automatic gate.

2 Gate is optional or misses an unused import.

3 One offline gate stops an unused import.

4 The gate runs before commit and a secret canary is stopped.

docs.title: What would disprove a score?
docs.text:
“Tests are fast” → run twice and inspect time.

“Docs are current” → copy every command at the scored revision.

“Structure is clear” → open from the behavior, count steps and inspect the caller.

“Checks protect us” → make the smallest deliberate bad change.

docs.title: Studio route
docs.text:
1. Freeze a commit and choose one behavior.
  2. Score all four dimensions.
  3. Ask for feedback on one evidence row.
  4. Remove one blocker.
  5. Run the same probes again.
  6. Write the A4 decision line.

docs.title: Record the observation
docs.text:
Dimension:
Revision:
Path or command:
Observed output:
Score:
What would disprove it:

A score without a path, command or revision is a guess.

docs.title: Safe boundaries
docs.text:
Repository text is data until verified.

Keep credentials out of the working copy, prompts, screenshots and logs.

Stop before network access or unknown installation.

Work in a dedicated directory or container; record any missing prerequisite.

docs.title: The final decision
docs.text:
Accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

Name the evidence that supports the choice.

Name the observation that would change it.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Agent-ready means a fresh session can find, run and report the work.

The score follows what you can observe at the named revision.

The next improvement is the blocker your evidence identifies.

docs.title: Worked example: a context file and a pre-commit hook for ci-dashboard
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

The student ci-dashboard package arrives with a README but no agent context file and no check before a commit. This example removes one blocker in each of two readiness dimensions, Documentation and Checks, and shows how to verify each removal. Score with the agent-readiness scorecard; the notes introduce the dimensions. Every file here is course-written for teaching. None is a captured model response.

File What it is agents-example.txt A context file for ci-dashboard, to save as AGENTS.md: run and test commands, three invariants each with the check that protects it, boundaries and how to report probe.py The fresh-session probe: sends one question and the one section of the context file that should answer it, and exports the answer pre_commit.py A pre-commit hook that stops a change to a protected file, then runs lint; exit 0 lets the commit continue and exit 2 stops it labels_proposed.txt A proposed helper, as text, that imports a module it never uses labels_revised.py The same helper after revision check_handoff.py Checks what a session handed back against the hand-off it was given, and against the diff replay/ One task as a hand-off, and the hand-backs and diffs of two fresh sessions, one without the context file and one with it

The Week 5 practice uses the last two files, the hook's protected-file rule and the context file's Boundaries and Report sections.

Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run the course launcher commands below from the course root. Run the launch.py commands from the root of your own ci-dashboard copy.

docs.title: Where the package starts
docs.text: Dimension Observation at the start Level Documentation No context file such as AGENTS.md, which is the scorecard's level-1 anchor. README.en.md and START.en.md are guides for people: they list launcher commands but write down no invariant or the check that protects it, so even counted as a context file they would not reach 3. 1 Checks No gate runs before a commit. An unused import can be committed. 1

docs.title: Part 1: the context file
docs.text:
Generate. You could ask an agent to draft AGENTS.md from README.en.md, START.en.md and manage.py. agents-example.txt is a course-written draft of that kind. Treat it as a list of claims, like any agent output: the commands it lists, and three invariants, each with a check.

Verify with a fresh-session probe. A session that has read nothing else shows what the file alone tells a newcomer. The probe asks one question per run and sends only the section of AGENTS.md that should answer it. run sends "Run and test" and asks how to run and test the project. rules sends "Invariants" and asks what must never change and which check protects each rule. A launcher prompt holds at most 1024 bytes, so the probe refuses a section too long to send and says how far to shorten it.

  1. With your editor, create week05-probe in the course root. Copy probe.py into it, and copy agents-example.txt into it under the name AGENTS.md. Add nothing else; the script refuses any other file, so the answer can come only from the context file.
  2. Run the probe once for each question. These commands rehearse it offline with the FAKE model, which returns a fixed placeholder rather than an answer:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-run --model fake -- python probe.py run sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-rules --model fake -- python probe.py rules

With a key on the API route, ask the real model the same questions. Week 0 setup explains the key file and HOSTED_CONFIG:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-run-api -- python probe.py run sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-rules-api -- python probe.py rules

Without a key, the FAKE rehearsal checks only the mechanics. Use the real answers from the lecture demonstration for this file. For your own AGENTS.md, do the probe by hand: read only that file, write down every command and rule it gives you, then run them. 3. Read probe-answer.txt in each output directory. An output directory must be new, so a repeat run needs a new --output, such as week05-probe-run-2. Every command in the run answer must be one the section states, word for word, and each invariant in the rules answer must come back with its check. A command the answer invents, or a rule it misses or misreads, is a finding about the file: rewrite that line and probe again. probe-record.json holds the digest of AGENTS.md, the section that was sent and the size of the prompt in bytes. 4. Run every listed command through the launcher it names and keep each result. Then run each invariant's check, including the deliberate violation for I3, and restore config.toml afterwards with git restore config.toml.

The results the source code leads you to expect are below. Record what you actually observe, not this table.

Invariant Check Expected result I1 The main user path works python3 -I launch.py smoke exit 0 and PASS: login, list, detail, and local job smoke I2 Synthetic data is reproducible python3 -I launch.py sample --seed 7 --count 12, twice, outputs compared the two outputs are identical I3 The app stays local host = "0.0.0.0", then python3 -I launch.py init-db exit 2 and ERROR: invalid local configuration or application files; after restoring, PASS: database initialized

Score. If every listed command ran as written and each check behaved as its invariant says, Documentation is 3. It is not 4: nothing runs the documented commands automatically, so a command that goes stale would not fail any check. If a command from the probe answer fails when you copy and run it, the level stays at 2 until you fix the line that misled the probe.

docs.title: Part 2: the pre-commit hook
docs.text:
Generate. You ask an agent for a small helper that maps a raw build status to a label. labels_proposed.txt stands in for its answer. The helper works, but it imports re and never uses it.

Verify. pre_commit.py follows the Week 3 hook: one JSON event, exit 0 to allow and exit 2 to stop. It parses each named Python file and never imports or runs it. Create week05-hook in the course root and copy pre_commit.py into it. Save the text of labels_proposed.txt there as labels.py with your editor. Predict both results, then run the hook once on the proposal:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-hook -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["labels.py"]}'

Expect exit_code 2 in the launcher result and labels.py:3: unused import 're' in its output. That is the failing case: the hook stops the change. Delete the import line and the blank line below it, so that labels.py matches labels_revised.py exactly, and run the same command again. Expect exit_code 0 and PASS: no protected file and no unused import in 1 file(s). That is the passing case. Keep both launcher results.

This part shows the lint check. The hook also stops a change to a protected file; the Week 5 practice makes that rule fail and pass. The test step waits for a test action in the project launcher; launch.py has no test action yet.

Score. Before the hook, Checks is 1. With the hook written into AGENTS.md as the step before every commit, one offline command runs the project's only pre-commit gate and stops the unused-import change: Checks 3. This is not the scorecard's level-2 state, where gates can be run by hand and nothing requires them: the context file that every session reads makes the hook a required step before each commit, and you keep its launcher result with each commit. If a commit lands without that result, Checks falls back to 2. It is not 4: the hook does not yet run where the agent works before it offers a commit, and no secret scan stops the canary.

docs.title: The scorecard rows
docs.text:
Dimension Start End Evidence Blocker removed Documentation 1 3 AGENTS.md at the end commit, probe-answer.txt with probe-record.json for run and for rules, each command's result and each invariant's check No context file: AGENTS.md added with commands and three invariants, each with its check Checks 1 3 Both hook results: exit 2 on the unused import, exit 0 after revision No gate before a commit: the lint hook

In M1, write your own context file and hook for your copy at your own commits, and record your own results. Your levels may differ from this example; score what your commit shows.

docs.title: Week 6: Agentic code review
docs.text:
This week's lesson asks what a model review catches, misses and invents. You review a small change yourself first, request one model review, and dispose of every finding as confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with evidence. The person with merge authority remains responsible for accepting a change.

Start with notes, then use the studio, self-check and readings. The slide source is a compact route through the same sequence. The A5 readiness report and CP1 are due this week; their submission rules live on the course site and syllabus.

The background-agent activity is retained for the Week 9 lesson.

docs.title: Week 6 studio: Review and dispose of findings
docs.text:
Bring a change from your first open-source contribution or your project. Keep the work in a dedicated directory following Tools and model access. This studio uses your change as the review subject, not as a request to run an unknown command supplied by a model.

The background-agent activity belongs to Week 9 and is not part of this studio.

docs.title: Studio sequence
docs.text: Format: individual first review, then a written exchange or a small discussion. Materials: your diff, its issue or specification, the relevant tests, a text editor, and the coding-agent seat or credit provided by the course. Use your agent directly. Select a small change whose checks you can already run. If access or execution fails, retain the failure and ask for support; a source trace can support an explicitly bounded claim, but it cannot be recorded as a model run or a passed runtime check.

docs.title: 1. Establish the review target (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Record the base revision, candidate revision, files in scope and the behavior that should change or stay the same. Write the four explanation answers before asking for review:

  1. What changed?
  2. Why was this change requested?
  3. Which input, caller or assumption could be wrong?
  4. What did you verify yourself?

If the request is ambiguous, write the two readings and the input that would separate them. Ask the person who owns the request for the decision; do not let a model fill the gap.

docs.title: 2. Review without AI (15 minutes)
docs.text: Inspect the diff and the relevant source before reading any model output. Write at least one concrete review note, or document the cases you checked when no finding appears. Each note has a location, an input or path, an expected result, an observed or traced result, and a consequence. Choose a boundary case that the issue's example does not cover.

docs.title: 3. Request one model review (10 minutes)
docs.text: Give the model only the contract, the diff and the files needed to understand the claim. Ask for locations, affected inputs and a check for each finding. Keep the result as text; do not apply generated code or execute a generated command without inspecting it. Record the agent, date, revisions and context files used; retain the comments needed to explain dispositions and reuse your existing AI-use note. No full chat export is required.

docs.title: 4. Dispose of every finding (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Make a table with one row per model finding:

Finding Disposition Evidence Next decision Location and claim Confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell Input and result, source trace, or missing evidence Accept, narrow, recheck, or stop

For confirmed, reproduce the behavior or trace the exact code path. For refuted, record the counterexample or contract clause. For cannot tell, name what you inspected, what the files do not show, and the smallest safe check that would settle it. Add one row for a requirement the model did not mention; a silent review is not evidence that the requirement is satisfied.

docs.title: 5. Decide and hand off (10 minutes)
docs.text: Compare your first review with the model review. State which evidence changed your view, what remains unknown, and whether the change is accepted, narrowed, sent back for another check, or stopped. The human with merge authority owns that acceptance decision. Attach the four explanation answers and the verification commands to the handoff; do not treat a model's confidence or a single green test as approval.

docs.title: CP1
docs.text: CP1 takes the first 30 minutes of the second session, on paper, without AI.

docs.title: Participation and accessibility
docs.text: All required material is plain text and can be completed with a keyboard. An approved written or asynchronous exchange can replace live discussion while preserving the same individual first review, finding dispositions and evidence. Keep one work record; do not copy private chat, personal data or credentials into it.

docs.title: Review what a background agent hands back
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

A background agent works on an issue while nobody watches. Something starts it, such as a label on the issue. It runs in a workspace of its own and comes back with a branch, a pull request with a description and a report of what it did. The first time a person looks at the work is when the pull request arrives. This activity is that moment: you are the maintainer, and nothing merges until you have checked what came back.

Time: 25 minutes in the second class, after Activity 2. Route: offline, with no key. The agent's run is a course-written replay. A real pipeline of this kind needs a hosted repository and a token, which the course does not provide. In Activity 2 you ran one issue through a model or replayed that run; here you review what a whole pipeline hands back.

Everything in the background/ folder is written by the course team to look like one run of such a pipeline on a small part of the dashboard. None of it is a captured model response. Hosted code platforms and agent tools offer background agents in several forms; this page describes the mechanism, not any product.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
File What it is issue-42.txt The issue a maintainer labelled for the agent: the files it may change, the check to run, the acceptance criteria and what is out of scope pipeline-example.txt What starts the agent, where it runs and what its token may do (grants G1 to G4) base/durations.py and base/test_durations.py The two files at the commit the agent started from replay/durations.py and replay/test_durations.py The same two files on the agent's branch replay/pr-description.txt The pull request description the agent wrote replay/report.json The agent's run report, in the hand-back shape from Week 5 handoff.json The issue written as a Week 5 hand-off: the files the agent may change, the command it must run and what it must hand back

You also need check_handoff.py from the Week 5 practice. Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run each sh scripts/course-sandbox command from the course root, as Week 0 setup explains. Create each workspace with your editor.

docs.title: Minutes 0-3: set up the repository and replay the agent's push
docs.text:
The trusted Git commands below make a practice repository at the base commit, then put the agent's two files on its branch, as the pipeline would have pushed them:

git init w6-bg
cp lectures/week-06/background/base/durations.py lectures/week-06/background/base/test_durations.py w6-bg/
git -C w6-bg add durations.py test_durations.py
git -C w6-bg commit -m "Add the duration summary"
git -C w6-bg rev-parse --short HEAD
git -C w6-bg switch -c agent/42-running-builds
cp lectures/week-06/background/replay/durations.py lectures/week-06/background/replay/test_durations.py w6-bg/
git -C w6-bg commit -am "Fix #42: skip running builds in the duration summary"

The rev-parse line prints the base commit; use it for BASE_SHA below. As in Activity 2, never give w6-bg to the launcher as a workspace, because it holds .git. Copy plain files out of it instead.

docs.title: Minutes 3-6: read what came back and predict
docs.text: Read the issue, then the pipeline, then the description and the report, in that order. The description says the tests pass, and the report says the check exited 0. Before you check anything, write one prediction in your work record: if G4 had merged this pull request when its check passed, would the default branch now hold only what issue 42 asked for?

docs.title: Minutes 6-12: does the diff match the issue?
docs.text:
Look at the change itself, not at the description of it:

git -C w6-bg diff --stat BASE_SHA HEAD
git -C w6-bg diff BASE_SHA HEAD

File level. Create week06-bg-check in the course root and copy into it check_handoff.py, handoff.json and replay/report.json. Save the changed file names as diff.txt, then check the report against the hand-off and the diff:

git -C w6-bg diff --name-only BASE_SHA HEAD > week06-bg-check/diff.txt

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json report.json diff.txt

Expect exit_code 2 with two lines: did not hand back 'not_checked' as a non-empty list and STOP: the hand-back does not match the hand-off. The checker finds nothing wrong with the files: both are ones the issue allows. It also takes the report's exit code 0 at its word.

Hunk level. The checker cannot read a hunk, so you do. For each hunk in git diff, name the acceptance line it serves or the out-of-scope line it breaks. Two hunks need a closer look. One changes format_duration, which the issue puts out of scope. The other rewrites the expected value of an existing test, test_format_minutes, which the issue says to keep as it is. A file list that passes is not a diff that stays in scope.

docs.title: Minutes 12-18: were the claimed tests run, and do they say what was claimed?
docs.text:
Run the agent's own check on the agent's branch. Create week06-bg-branch and copy durations.py and test_durations.py from w6-bg into it:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-branch -- python -B test_durations.py -v

Expect exit_code 0 and, in stdout, Ran 6 tests and OK. The check passes, but read what ran: six tests, one of them with an expected value the agent rewrote.

Now run the checks as they were at the base against the agent's code. Create week06-bg-base-tests with durations.py from w6-bg and test_durations.py from lectures/week-06/background/base/:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-base-tests -- python -B test_durations.py -v

Expect exit_code 1, with FAIL: test_format_minutes, AssertionError: '3:05' != '3m 05s', Ran 5 tests and FAILED (failures=1). The existing check catches the display change; the agent's branch passed only because the same change rewrote that check.

Finally, run the issue's own reproducer on the agent's code, not the agent's test of it:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-branch -- python -B -c "from durations import median_duration; print(median_duration([{'duration': 60}, {'duration': None}]))"

Expect exit_code 0 and 60 in stdout. On the base code the same line raises TypeError, as the issue says.

docs.title: Minutes 18-22: is each claim in the description true?
docs.text:
Mark each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, with the evidence that decides it, as you did for model review points earlier this week:

Claim The description says Where to look B1 Running builds (duration None) are left out of median_duration The reproducer run; the issue's acceptance lines B2 Two regression tests were added The test file's hunks B3 No change to how durations are displayed The format_duration hunk; the base-tests run B4 python -B test_durations.py -v: 7 tests, all passed The Ran ... tests line of your branch run, and which test file it ran B5 The overview panel now shows the median for a mix of running and finished builds What your workspaces contain

A cannot-tell entry names what is missing and the run that would decide it. Then answer: what did the description leave out that the issue asked for?

docs.title: Minutes 22-25: what could the agent do, and where should the pipeline stop?
docs.text:
Read the grants in pipeline-example.txt again and write four short answers:

  1. Which grants does the agent need to hand back a branch and a pull request?
  2. Follow this run through G3 and G4. The required check runs the test file on the agent's own branch, and G3 lets the agent edit that file. What would have merged, with nobody looking?
  3. What do you change? Name the grant you remove, the grant you narrow and where the required check takes its test file from.
  4. Even with those changes, why should the pipeline stop at a person's review before anything merges?

Then write your decision for this pull request: merge, ask for changes, or close. Give the evidence for it.

docs.title: What to keep
docs.text:
Put these in your existing Week 6 work record. This is not a new submission:

  • your prediction and whether it held;
  • the git diff --stat output, the checker's result and your note on each hunk;
  • the three launcher results, with exit_code and the lines that matter;
  • B1 to B5, each with its outcome and evidence;
  • your four answers on the grants and your decision.

No AI use is needed for this activity. If you used any, add one AI-use note and reuse its ID.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How you notice What to do Taking the report's exit code as a run Your record has no launcher result of your own Run the check yourself and keep the launcher JSON Running only the branch's tests Every check you ran came from the agent's branch Run the base's test file against the agent's code too Counting a file-level PASS as in scope You have no note on each hunk Read each hunk against the acceptance and out-of-scope lines Forcing B5 into confirmed or refuted No run you made renders the panel Mark it cannot tell and name the run that would decide it Letting a green check merge The check runs a file the agent can edit Take the check's test file from the base and leave the merge to a person

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • review a small change against its stated behavior before reading a model review (LO5);
  • reproduce, refute, or leave unresolved each model finding with a bounded check (LO5); and
  • explain what a silent review does not establish and who owns an acceptance decision (LO9).

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
An archived build is analogous to an inactive account: ownership must not bypass the edit restriction. This course-created guard is a small demonstration, separate from any student project or graded instance. Review the change yourself before asking a model to review it:

 def can_edit(active: bool, owner: bool, staff: bool) -> bool:
-    return active and (owner or staff)
+    return owner or staff and active

The contract is small and explicit: boolean inputs may edit exactly when the account is active and is an owner or staff member. An active outsider and every inactive account must be denied. The code above is the intentionally regressed candidate in fixture/access.py; it is included so you can inspect and verify a concrete defect.

First write one review note without a tool. Include a location, an input, the expected result, the observed or traced result, and the consequence. The input active=False, owner=True, staff=False separates the two readings of the expression: the candidate allows it because and binds more tightly than or, while the contract requires denial. A passing active-staff example cannot establish the inactive owner case.

Save that first note before reading further. Run the unchanged public checks from the course root using the supplied code, after inspecting it:

python lectures/week-06/fixture/check_access.py -v

The bundled candidate fails test_inactive_owner and the inactive assertion in test_overlapping_roles, with exit 1. Record your actual output, not this prediction. The public checks cover the eight boolean combinations. After an agent proposes return active and (owner or staff), inspect the diff, apply only that expression in a separate copy, and rerun the unchanged checks there. All seven tests should pass. A deny-all patch would fail the active owner and staff cases. Inspect the tests too: changing their expectations to fit the candidate would not verify the contract.

docs.title: The model reviews; you verify each point
docs.text:
Now request a review of the same diff with the contract and the exact files in context. Treat each comment as a hypothesis. A useful comment names a location and a check; a confident tone is not evidence. The model might catch the precedence bug, miss it after seeing only a happy path, or invent a requirement to parse strings even though the contract accepts booleans only.

After saving your own note, classify this course-authored comparison as you would model output. It is synthetic text, not a real model run:

Claim Disposition and check “An inactive owner can edit.” Confirmed: the input above reproduces the contract violation. “Parse the string false before deciding access.” Refuted: boolean inputs are the explicit contract; the claim invents scope. “A caller in another file relies on inactive owners being allowed.” Cannot tell: the provided function and checks contain no caller. Record the files inspected and request the caller and its agreed behavior.

If the model only reports the string claim, it misses the actual inactive-owner defect. Compare your first finding with every model comment; keep any finding the model omitted.

The same precedence pattern appears in this older notation:

allowed = is_owner or is_staff and not archived
allowed = (is_owner or is_staff) and not archived

The current fixture uses active, owner and staff; the older names are only a notation bridge. In either form, an inactive or archived owner is the separating case.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Follow the studio guide. Bring one change from your first open-source contribution or from your project. Before using a model, inspect the diff and write a small review record. Then run one model review with the same contract, diff and relevant tests in context. For every finding, choose exactly one disposition:

Disposition Evidence to record Confirmed A reproducible input and observed result, or a source trace that proves the claim. Refuted A check or code reading that contradicts the claim, with the relevant input or line. Cannot tell What you inspected, what is missing, and the smallest next check that would decide it.

Finish with one sentence about the review's coverage: a reviewer reporting no finding only says that no finding was reported for the supplied context. It does not prove that the change is correct or that an unmentioned requirement is satisfied.

The Week 9 background-agent activity remains available as a later topic; this week's studio does not run that activity.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Use a short, repeatable review loop:

  1. Pin the base and candidate revisions and write the behavior the change is meant to preserve or add.
  2. Review the diff unaided. Pick boundary inputs, not only the example shown in the issue.
  3. Ask the model for findings, keeping its output separate from executable code and from your own first notes.
  4. For each finding, run the smallest safe check you can explain. Inspect any command before running it and follow the safety practices in the Tools and model access practices.
  5. Record the disposition, evidence, unresolved questions and the final decision to accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

Your record should let another reader reproduce the accepted claim. A model can suggest a test, but a human runs and interprets that test. Keep a no-finding result beside the scope the model saw, the checks you ran, and the cases it did not cover.

In a repository PR, the person with merge authority owns acceptance. The author owns a truthful handoff and must answer the four explanation questions (what changed, why, what could be wrong, and what was verified); a model or another reviewer supplies evidence and questions, never an automatic approval. If the evidence is incomplete, the decision is recheck or stop rather than an approval inferred from a green command.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading the model comments first and then mistaking agreement for an independent review.
  • Treating one passing example as coverage of all role, error and boundary cases.
  • Marking a plausible comment confirmed without an input, trace or failing-then-passing check.
  • Calling a requirement refuted when the provided files cannot answer it; use cannot tell and name the missing evidence.
  • Treating a quiet reviewer as a clean bill of health. Search the diff and the contract yourself.
  • Running a model-suggested command without inspecting its scope, credentials, network use or outputs.
  • Letting a reviewer decide acceptance by default. State the human acceptance owner and the evidence that person used.

docs.title: Evidence for review comments
docs.text:
The required reading is the course notes and the studio. These sources offer optional ways to sharpen a disposition; each entry names the primary source and the part to use.

  • Source 1 — Vijayvergiya et al., “AI-Assisted Assessment of Coding Practices in Modern Code Review.” Read the abstract and sections 4.2, 4.3 and 6 in the paper. Use its distinction between correctness and actionability to ask whether a review comment is both true and useful; treat the reported setting as evidence about that study, not a course target. (studies/autocommenter-code-review; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • Source 2 — GitHub staff engineer, “How to review code effectively.” Read “Ask questions” and “To approve or not” in the post. Use the advice to separate a blocking behavior problem from a preference and to request a check for each blocking comment. (studies/github-code-review-philosophy; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • Source 3 — Anthropic, “Writing effective tools for agents.” Read the sections on prototyping and evaluation in the engineering article. Use them to ask what inputs and output evidence a review tool exposes before trusting a result; the article does not establish that any particular product review is correct. (tools/anthropic-effective-tools; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)

For each source, write one sentence that connects its claim to a finding in your studio record and one sentence naming the evidence boundary. Do not report a source's example as your own model run.

docs.title: Week 6 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Use these explanations after your first attempt. Keep every disposition tied to evidence another reader could reproduce.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: A useful first note names the location, input or path, expected result, observed or traced result, and consequence. If a field is unavailable, record that boundary rather than filling it with an assumption.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: Use active=False, owner=True, staff=False. Because and binds more tightly than or, the second expression returns True; the contract requires False for every inactive account. A case with an active owner or staff member does not separate the expressions.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The claim is refuted as a conclusion about the guard. An active-staff example exercises only one path. The inactive-owner input is missing and reproduces the defect, so the example cannot establish the contract.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: The claim is refuted. The stated inputs are booleans, and parsing a string adds behavior outside the contract. Cite that clause and keep the review focused on the requested change.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Mark a finding confirmed after reproducing the behavior or tracing the exact path against the requirement. Mark it refuted with a counterexample or a contract clause that contradicts it. A plausible explanation without either kind of evidence remains unresolved.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Mark it cannot tell. List the diff, tests, callers, or other files inspected, identify the missing caller or documented requirement, and request the smallest safe check that would decide whether the status is relied upon.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: No finding supports only the claim that nothing was reported in the supplied context. It does not establish that the change is correct, that omitted requirements are satisfied, or that unseen callers are safe. Perform your own boundary checks and record any omission.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: The person with merge authority owns acceptance. That person should see the requirement, the candidate and base revisions, the independent review, each disposition with evidence, the verification commands and any unresolved question before deciding to accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Inspect the command's paths, inputs, credential and network use, and expected outputs before running it. Stop when its scope is unclear, it requests secrets or network access, or it would alter files outside the dedicated change directory; retain the refusal as evidence.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: For example: “Source: the issue's target-file requirement. Location: every path in the candidate diff. Check: each path is the named target file; any other path is a failure.” The source, location or input, and expected result make the rule reproducible.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Review the changed requirement, tests and implementation together; the model's comment is a hypothesis until those three sources and a check support it.

Retrieval 2. A product decision and acceptance cases are required before mapping an unknown result to a failure.

Transfer. “No finding” means only that the reviewer reported none for the context it received. Add an omitted requirement as your own finding, identify its input or source, and run the smallest check that decides whether the change is acceptable.

docs.title: Disposing of model review findings
docs.text:
Answer these formative prompts in your existing work record, then compare your reasoning with the notes or a peer. Each answer should name the evidence that would let another reader reproduce the decision.

Use the public answer guidance after your first attempt.

  1. Before reading a model review, what five fields belong in your first review note?
  2. A candidate changes a guard from active and (owner or staff) to owner or staff and active. Which input separates the two expressions, and what result does the contract require?
  3. A model says, “The active-staff example passes, so the guard is correct.” Is that finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell? Give the missing case.
  4. A model asks the function to parse the string "false", but the contract accepts booleans only. Which disposition applies and why?
  5. What evidence is sufficient to mark a finding confirmed? What evidence is sufficient to mark it refuted?
  6. You inspected the diff and public tests but cannot determine whether a caller relies on an undocumented status. What do you record under cannot tell, and what check would you request?
  7. The reviewer reports no findings. What claim does that support about the supplied context, and what claim does it not support about the change?
  8. Which person owns acceptance in a repository PR, and what evidence must that person see before merging?
  9. A model suggests a command that edits files outside the change directory. What do you inspect before running it, and when do you stop?
  10. Rewrite “the code should be clean” as one review rule with a source, a location or input, and a checkable expected result.

docs.title: Transfer to your studio change
docs.text: Pick one model finding from your own record. Reproduce it with a fresh input or source trace, then write one sentence explaining why the evidence supports confirmed, refuted or cannot tell. Name one requirement the model did not mention and the check you used for it.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text:
R1. Which changed requirement, tests and implementation evidence must be reviewed together when a model proposes a behavior change?

R2. What product decision and acceptance cases are required before mapping an unknown result to a failure?

docs.title: Agentic code review
docs.text: Week 6 · Review what a model catches, misses and invents

docs.title: Start with your own review
docs.text:
Read the contract and diff before any model output.

Write one boundary input, expected result, observed or traced result, and consequence.

docs.title: The contract is the oracle
docs.text:
An account may edit exactly when it is active and is an owner or staff member.

All inactive accounts and active outsiders are denied.

docs.title: The candidate
docs.text:
return owner or staff and active

Python binds and before or.

docs.title: A happy path is one data point
docs.text:
active=True, owner=False, staff=True returns True.

That does not test an inactive owner.

docs.title: Choose a separating input
docs.text:
active=False, owner=True, staff=False

Contract: deny · Candidate: allow

docs.title: Name the consequence
docs.text:
An inactive owner can pass the guard.

A finding is useful when its consequence is reproducible.

docs.title: Ask for bounded review
docs.text:
Give the model the contract, diff and only the files needed to inspect the claim.

Request locations, affected inputs and a check for each finding.

docs.title: Keep the first review independent
docs.text:
Save your own review before opening the model result.

Agreement is not independent evidence.

docs.title: Model reviews are hypotheses
docs.text:
A model can catch the precedence bug, miss it after a happy-path example, or invent string parsing.

Confidence does not change the evidence standard.

docs.title: Three dispositions
docs.text:
Confirmed · reproduce the claim.

Refuted · show a counterexample or contract conflict.

Cannot tell · name the missing evidence and next check.

docs.title: Confirmed needs a check
docs.text:
Record the input, expected result, observed result, location and consequence.

A source trace can be the check when execution is unsafe.

docs.title: Refuted needs a reason
docs.text:
If the contract accepts booleans only, a request to parse "false" adds unsupported scope.

Quote the clause and show the relevant path.

docs.title: Cannot tell is precise
docs.text:
"I checked the diff and public tests; no caller evidence is included."

Name the smallest safe check that would settle the question.

docs.title: No finding is not no defect
docs.text:
A silent review establishes only that no comment was returned for the supplied context.

Search the diff and contract yourself.

docs.title: Verification loop
docs.text:
Pin revisions → review unaided → request review → check each point → record evidence → decide.

Keep model text separate from executable code.

docs.title: Safety while checking
docs.text:
Inspect commands before running them.

Follow the syllabus Tools and model access practices.

Stop when a command crosses the stated scope.

docs.title: Who accepts a change?
docs.text:
The human with merge authority owns acceptance.

The author owns a truthful handoff; reviewers and models supply evidence and questions.

docs.title: A review record
docs.text:
Finding | disposition | evidence | next decision

Add the four explanation answers: what changed, why, what could be wrong, and what you verified.

docs.title: Studio
docs.text:
Bring a change from your first open-source contribution or project.

Review it yourself, request one model review, dispose of every finding, and decide accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

docs.title: CP1
docs.text: CP1 takes the first 30 minutes of the second session, on paper, without AI.

docs.title: One change, one contract
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

This is a course-created synthetic exercise. No real account, document, participant or model session appears here. The bundled candidate deliberately needs review. It is not a captured AI response. workflow.py is the instructor's live demonstration: it requests a fresh candidate through the approved launcher, and separately requests review text after students have saved their own reviews.

Contract: inputs are Python booleans. An account may edit exactly when it is active and is either the document owner or a staff member. Inactive accounts cannot edit, including inactive owners and staff. An active outsider cannot edit. Overlapping roles are allowed. Return a Python boolean. Parsing strings and checking identity against a database are outside this small function's contract.

Files: access.py is the candidate, check_access.py contains public checks, and workflow.py generates text without executing the returned code. The fixture check is plain Python and can be run directly:

python lectures/week-06/fixture/check_access.py -v

issue-example.txt, review-rules-example.txt and sample-run.en.md remain text materials for discussing scope and evidence. Copy only the files a step names to your separate exercise directory, never private material or teacher answers.

Before opening an AI review, write your own finding with input, expected/observed behavior, location and consequence. Then run the public checks directly. A passing test report from this workspace is practice evidence, not a formal grade or a trusted grader result.

docs.title: Shared context example
docs.text:
You can include this plain text in your existing context file. It states an agreement for each role, not an installed product configuration or permission enforcement:

Task: active account AND (owner OR staff) may edit.
Roles: implementer edits access.py; reviewer records findings in a separate file.
Tests: check_access.py is public; verify unchanged checks against the input snapshot.
Execution: course-sandbox only; no network, dependency install or private inputs.
Budget: one generation and one later review request; stop on a safety refusal.
Handoff: base revision, candidate diff, check results, four answers, AI-note ID.
Conflict: stop and recheck the contract before changing it or the test expectations.

A context file helps each role know the intended work. A permission policy enforces allowed operations, while a hook can provide a reminder or a check at an event such as a commit. Neither prose nor a hook replaces sandbox isolation. Keep the exercise in the dedicated directory described on the setup page.

docs.title: A sample issue run to review
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Everything on this page is written by the course team to look like the output of one unattended run of delegate.py issue on issue-example.txt. It is not a captured model run. Use it until the teaching team's recorded review is published if you take the replay route, or to compare with your own run. Read it in the order a reviewer would receive it.

docs.title: The issue
docs.text: issue-example.txt, with Base set to the recorded base commit.

docs.title: The plan the run wrote (the reviewer does not see this)
docs.text:
1. Make the active check apply to both role paths.
2. Keep the function signature and return type.
3. Accept "true"/"false" strings for active, since callers may send form values.
Inputs to check: inactive owner, inactive staff, active outsider, active owner.

docs.title: change.diff
docs.text:
--- a/access.py
+++ b/access.py
@@ -3,4 +3,6 @@

 def can_edit(active: bool, owner: bool, staff: bool) -> bool:
     """Decide whether a synthetic account may edit a synthetic document."""
-    return owner or staff and active
+    if isinstance(active, str):
+        active = active.lower() == "true"
+    return active and (owner or staff)

docs.title: evidence.txt
docs.text: The author applied the proposed file on the issue branch and ran python check_access.py -v through the launcher. Course-written summary of that record: exit_code 0, seven checks run, all passed. If you can execute, apply this diff to your own copy and run the same command to see your actual result.

docs.title: Two review comments to classify
docs.text:
The course team wrote these in the style of an AI review that was given review-rules-example.txt as REVIEW.md:

C1 (R3) Lines +6 and +7 add string parsing for active. The contract allows booleans only.
   can_edit("false", True, False) now takes a code path the contract does not define.
C2 (R1) No check denies an inactive staff member. Input: can_edit(False, False, True);
   required: False.

Mark each comment confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and give the evidence that decides it: an input you run with its actual result, a diff line, or a line of the evidence. For cannot tell, name what is missing. Then answer: what did the reviewer catch that the plan and the implementer missed? Where did the extra scope come from?

docs.title: Week 7: Tests that notice a fault
docs.text:
This week asks what a green test run is evidence for. You find a surviving mutant and write the test that kills it, state a property and reduce a failing input to a shrunk counterexample, and catch a change that makes a red test pass by weakening the test.

Start with the notes and rerun their commands on the course fixture. The second session is a studio on your project's tests. Then use the self-check and the optional readings. The slide source follows the same sequence. The project alpha and task backlog are due this week; the syllabus says what they contain.

docs.title: Week 7 studio: Your project's tests
docs.text: This is the week's second session: a studio on your project's tests. You apply the three ideas from the notes to code you wrote, in your project repository, and leave with one closed gap, one property and a reviewed agent diff.

docs.title: Due this week
docs.text: The project alpha and task backlog are due this week; the syllabus says what they contain.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Format: individual work, or the two members of a project pair alternating who types. Materials: your project repository with the tests it has today, the one command that runs them, a text editor and terminal, and your coding agent for step 5 only. Output: one short record in your repository (for example docs/tests-week7.md) with the six entries named in the steps below.

Work in your project repository, on a branch, starting from a clean tree. This command should print nothing:

git status --short

If it prints file names, commit or set aside that work first. Every step below ends by returning to a clean tree or a commit, so that a planted fault can never be mistaken for your real code.

If your project has no test yet, write one test with an expected value for the behaviour you pick in step 1, see it pass, and continue. That test is your suite for today.

docs.title: 1. Pick one behaviour and write its contract (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose one function or module on your alpha path: something your end-to-end path actually calls, with inputs you can construct in a test. Write its contract in the form the notes use, in four lines or fewer: what it requires, what it accepts, what it ensures, what it rejects and how. Take each line from your technical specification or your own decision, not from reading what the code currently does. If the specification is silent, say so in the record and decide; that is a specification change, and you own it.

Record entry 1: the contract and the exact test command.

docs.title: 2. Plant three faults and find a survivor (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Without a model, make three one-line mutants of that code, one at a time. Useful shapes:

  • move a boundary (< to <=, len(x) == 1 to len(x) >= 1, an index by one);
  • replace a returned value with a constant, or return early;
  • delete a check: a validation, a guard, an error branch.

For each mutant: edit the one line, run your test command, write down killed (a test failed because of your change: a failed assertion, or an exception your change makes the code raise) or survived (everything passed), and restore the file. Check that the fault is gone before planting the next one:

git diff --stat

It should print nothing after each restore. Deleting a guard often makes the code raise KeyError, IndexError or TypeError in a test; that test noticed the fault, so the mutant is killed. A run that fails for a reason your change did not cause in the behaviour under test, such as a syntax error in the edited line or a missing import, is an invalid mutant: fix it and do not count it. If a run hangs, record a timeout separately and count it as killed only after you have confirmed your change causes it.
