docs.title: A UI change and one task check
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Course-authored files for the generate-then-verify example. No file calls a model, opens a network connection or writes a file. Read each one as text before running anything.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• current.html is the build page from the notes: Overview | Options | Refresh, with the status filter (State) inside the closed Options disclosure. The page has no script; the dashboard fills its rows.
  • agent-replay.json holds the request for a visible Status: All control and two recorded replies. They are a course-authored replay that stands in for an agent; no model wrote them. Each reply points to its page.
  • proposal-a.html and proposal-b.html are the two proposed pages. Compare each with current.html using diff -u.
  • dashboard.py holds eight synthetic builds and the unchanged query. A higher build number is more recent. The page shows the first two rows of the result, and the dashboard reads only the pipeline and status fields of a request.
  • check_task.py tries the task "Find the most recent failed build in pipeline Alpha." on one page and prints what it did.
  • rehearsal.html is a second page for the same task, with the status filter placed differently. The workshop uses it for the observation rehearsal, so the person trying the task has not seen it in class. If you are that person, do not open it before the rehearsal.
  • org-portal.json, org-gateway.json, org-changes.json and org-routes.json hold the replayed records for the organization practice: a portal's grants and one agent session, a gateway policy and six runs, the runs and review minutes behind four changes, and a routing policy with its evaluator results. Each holds an agent_summary that stands in for an agent's report; no model wrote it.
  • org_check.py checks one of those files and prints what it found; it is described under Organization practice below.

docs.title: What the check does
docs.text:
The check is a task-completion script with a keyboard and accessible-name check built in. Its simulated user follows one narrow strategy:

  1. It presses Tab from the top of the page. Content inside a closed disclosure is not reached.
  2. It opens a disclosure, or chooses a select option, only when its text shares a word with the task (failed, build, pipeline, alpha). It does not follow links.
  3. It activates the first reachable submit button. The form sends its named fields as a browser would, including fields inside closed disclosures, and the unchanged query answers. If a field is sent more than once, the dashboard reads its first value, and the output lists the field under fields sent more than once.

The task counts as completed when the first row shown is build #121, the most recent failed build in pipeline Alpha, and every control it reached has an accessible name. The script also runs the unchanged query once on its own, so you can see that the query check passes on every page. It exits 0 when the task is completed and the query check passes, and 1 when either fails: a completed task does not excuse a broken query.

The check reads HTML as text and never runs it, so the unchanged course file runs on the host with the locked course tools, like the Week 11 replay. Do not edit check_task.py or dashboard.py; change only a copy of an HTML page. Code that a model proposes for your own project still runs only through the launcher described in Week 0 setup.

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py --view lectures/week-13/fixture/current.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/current.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-a.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-b.html

--view prints only what a keyboard user meets when the page loads: the Tab order, each control's accessible name and the rows shown. It does not try the task, so a partner can use it for the observation rehearsal without seeing a result. If the partner opens a control, the observer reads them what is inside it from the page and records the action and their words.

docs.title: Expected distinction
docs.text:
• current.html: the State control is not reached, the request sends status=all, the first row is #123 running, and the task is not completed. The check exits 1.
  • proposal-a.html: the new Status control is reached, labelled and set to Failed, and the query check passes. The request sends state=failed, a field the dashboard ignores, so the first row is still #123 running. The task is not completed and the check exits 1.
  • proposal-b.html: the request sends status=failed, the first row is #121 failed, and the check exits 0.

Proposal A is the change that looks right and does not help: its diff, its label and the query check all pass, and only the task check shows that the selection never reaches the query.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The strategy matches words literally. A person may understand Status without the word failed, or miss a control the script finds. A completed run shows that the task can be done this way on this page; it does not show that people understand the label. That still needs a new observed session on the same revision. The check does not model CSS, scripts, pointer use or a screen reader's exact speech, and it reads only pages whose elements are explicitly closed.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
Each pair does one variation; the workshop does not ask for more. Copy one page, change one thing, and before you run the check on your copy, write the output line you expect to change and what you expect it to say:

  • remove the <label> for Status in a copy of proposal-b.html;
  • add aria-hidden="true" to that select;
  • remove the hidden pipeline field from a copy of proposal-b.html;
  • in a copy of proposal-a.html, change the new select's name="state" to name="status";
  • in a copy of current.html, rename the Options summary to Failed builds filter.

Keep the prediction beside the output. If they differ, find the line of the page or of the check that you misread before you try another change.

docs.title: Organization practice
docs.text:
org_check.py reads one JSON file, uses only the Python standard library and writes nothing. Its four commands apply one stated rule each:

  • portal replays each call through the grants: a call is allowed when a grant for its tool names its repository, or every repository with *. It then lists what each grant can reach and marks the repositories the task does not need. It exits 1 when any grant reaches beyond the task.
  • gateway replays each run through the policy: a request is refused before it is sent when it would exceed the request cap, when the tokens already used plus its own reservation would exceed the token cap, or when its route is not listed; when the provider is unavailable, the policy's fallback must answer. It also searches every sandbox-side line for the key. It exits 1 when a recorded decision differs from the policy or the key appears.
  • cost adds the units of every run, including failed, retried and rejected ones, and every review minute, then divides each total by the number of accepted changes. It prints one run's trace total beside the result. It exits 1 only when no change was accepted.
  • route supports a chosen route only when its evaluator results are for the route's current revision and it fails no case that the current route passes. It exits 1 when any choice is not supported.

Run it through the launcher, as the organization route shows. A command exits 2 when its file is missing a field or holds a value of the wrong kind. The records are synthetic, so a result is evidence about the rule you applied, not about any real portal, gateway or route.

docs.text:
Minutes Action Retained work 0-8 Locate one existing reference for each required discussion area An index into existing work, not a new report 8-16 Explain one need, source decision and discriminating check A concise causal account 16-24 Peer changes the role policy, the evaluation question or the rollback observation Independent reasoning about the new condition 24-32 Rehearse the visible feature and a permitted labelled fallback Current revision and honest limits 32-44 Predict the regression gate's exit code on the agent's evaluator change, watch the live run, then judge the model audit with the synthetic counts Your prediction beside the gate's exit codes; a bounded judgment for the Evaluate and Audit stages 44-54 Judge three stages of your own pipeline against the software-factory claim, using your own M3 counts for the Audit stage; a partner challenges one stage you marked unattended Stage, evidence reference, unattended now or not yet, and the check or stop rule that would change it 54-60 Revise one unsupported claim and check appointment details A revised explanation and confirmed participation plan

At the first feedback checkpoint, ask for a hint if the input, required effect or next observation remains unclear. docs.title: Week 14: Demonstrate and defend the result
docs.text: This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
Rehearse one engineering claim with visible verification, then explain a new input or failure independently. Explain the reasoning independently (LO1, LO2, LO3, LO4, LO5, LO6, LO7, LO8, LO9).

All examples, counts and files on this page are course-authored synthetic practice.

docs.title: A public defense practice packet
docs.text:
The agreed policy permits an edit exactly when owner or staff is true and archived is false. Guest means both role booleans are false. The packet continues the Week 6 dashboard case, whose earlier guard, is_owner or is_staff and not archived, let an archived owner edit. The repaired guard groups the two roles:

allowed = (is_owner or is_staff) and not archived
if allowed:
    title = requested_title

The supplied synthetic evidence matrix contains active owner/allow/New, active staff/allow/New, archived owner/deny/Old and archived staff/deny/Old. Guest cases are absent. Predict an active guest's decision and final title before reading on.

The code predicts denial and unchanged title for a guest, but the provided matrix has not observed it. State that distinction and propose the guest request with both response and state assertions. If those checks then complete on the repaired guard, acceptance can extend to those checked cases. A phrase such as "all permission boundaries are safe" would exceed this packet. These are public formative prompts, not the defense bank.

docs.title: Explain the cause, not only the result
docs.text: A concise account links a user need to a source change, discriminating check and revision: archived content needs protection; the old owner term bypassed archive; the new grouping applies archive to both roles; the archived-owner regression checks denial and unchanged state. Use actual references to your own work in the defense. A complete spoken explanation does not create missing evidence.

docs.title: Locate the existing work across the required areas
docs.text:
Discussion area Existing work to locate Public practice variation Requirements/acceptance M0 need, consented discovery and criterion Staff may now edit archived builds; owners who are not staff still may not. Which cases change? Evaluation M2 task/environment/agent/scorer and declared outcomes The question changes from "is the status exactly failed?" to "did the build finish without passing?", and the environment now includes canceled builds. Which oracle, cases and earlier results change? Security M1 regressions and M3/M4 audit response Add a guest input and check both response and state. Deployment/recovery M2 event chain, rollback and recovery assertions A rollback command reports success, and no request has reached the service since. Which states of the running service remain possible?

A changed question needs a new accepted contract and corresponding scorer cases: canceled now requires yes, running still requires no, and an earlier pass remains evidence for the old question only. A rollback's success message describes the command, not the running service: the previous revision may be serving, or the faulty revision may still be serving. Observe the running service itself, then one user request, before declaring recovery. A changed role policy requires its own authorization and cases rather than silently rewriting the previous expectations. The student answers new variations independently.

docs.title: A demonstration with an honest fallback
docs.text:
Your M4 demonstration takes place at the expo in the Week 14 workshop. Everyone demonstrates at the same time while staff and classmates move between stations and ask questions, and each student answers at least one staff question. The M4 section of the project guide says what to demonstrate. The expo does not replace your individually scheduled defense.

Show one user task, its visible behavior and the check that supports it. Identify the actual revision and explain a decision and remaining limit. If the live path fails, retain that result and state the next observation; use a labelled recording only if the announced format permits it. Do not relabel an older result as current.

A later task taking less time than an earlier one does not isolate an agent's productivity effect: difficulty, familiarity and prior practice may differ. Explain a prediction mismatch from your actual work without inventing causal measurement.

docs.title: The software factory is a claim to test
docs.text:
A software factory is an engineering concept that organizes requirements, generation, verification and delivery into a repeatable production process. This lecture tests the stronger claim that its stages could run with little human input. Treat that as a claim, not a conclusion. You can test it on the one pipeline you know in detail: your own ci-dashboard work. Split the pipeline into stages. For each stage, ask whether it could run unattended and what evidence would be needed first.

Stage Course evidence you already hold What must be shown before the stage runs unattended Specify M0 acceptance criteria; the user tests begun in Week 11 The criteria were executable, and the user tests found no need they missed Change M1 reviewed change; P2 review Review checks find the faults a person found, on changes that the reviewer did not author Test Week 7 surviving mutant, property and fuzz input The tests fail on meaningful faults, not only on the cases they were written for Evaluate M2 evaluator challenged in Week 10 The scorer has been challenged and still holds; Unknown is never counted as a pass Protect M1 security regressions from Week 8 The inert attack stays blocked and permitted work still succeeds Deploy and recover M2 incident drill from Week 11 Rollback and the recovery check, including the user's view, run without a person Audit Your verification of the teaching team's model audit on your frozen snapshot, M4 responses Each finding is marked confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with evidence, and no confirmed finding is one your own checks should have caught

docs.title: A gate that has been seen to fail
docs.text:
The Evaluate stage already has an executable gate: run-regression.sh from the evaluator kit, the local gate from the M2 evaluator workshop. It copies only evaluator.py and verify.py into a fresh workspace, runs verify.py through the launcher and exits with the candidate's status. The lecture runs it on the Week 14 fixture: an evaluator for the Week 10 contract, "is a supplied status exactly failed?", and nine frozen cases.

Generation: an agent proposes a change to the evaluator. The proposal, proposed_evaluator.py, is a course-authored replay; no model wrote it. Its reply says: "Made scoring robust to formatting. Answers are trimmed and lower-cased, and an answer that starts with the expected word now counts." Would an unattended pipeline merge it? Predict the gate's exit code before the run.

Verification: the instructor runs the gate on the proposal and then on the current evaluator, with the commands in the fixture README. With the proposal, the launcher record shows "exit_code": 1, the gate exits 1, and the record's stdout names the cases that failed:

{"cases": 9, "failed": [{"case": "extra_text", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}, {"case": "case_changed", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}

With the current evaluator the gate exits 0 and the failed list is empty. The proposal made formatting "robust" by accepting yes; mark this as passed, the Week 10 answer that tried to talk the scorer into a pass. The gate stopped it because a frozen case had been written for exactly that answer. If the record shows the launcher's generic "status": "failed" instead, the launcher refused the run: keep that result, and do not count it as the gate catching anything.

A stage runs unattended only with two kinds of evidence: a check seen to fail on a bad change and pass on a good one, run from cases the changing agent cannot edit, with the candidate scored in a separate process, and a stop path that someone has exercised. The demonstration shows the check failing and passing, but in a pipeline the cases would sit where the agent could edit them, the candidate runs inside the checker, and the stop path is untried. So the Evaluate stage is a candidate for merging evaluator changes unattended, not yet unattended. At least three things are still missing:

  • Cases the changing agent cannot edit. The gate copies verify.py from the same workspace as the candidate. In the demonstration it came from the fixture, which the replayed change did not touch. An agent that can rewrite the cases can make any change pass, so the gate must read verify.py from a location the agent cannot write, not from the candidate's workspace.
  • A candidate scored in its own process. verify.py imports the candidate and calls it in the same process. The candidate runs inside the process that checks it, so it can end the run or print its own report. An unattended gate must score the candidate in a separate process and treat that process's output only as data.
  • The stop rule exercised once. The stop rules say that any failed case, any refused cap or any rollback stops the agent and pages its owner. Someone has to see a failed gate run actually halt the merge and reach the owner; naming the rule is not exercising it.

The nine cases also have a limit. A change that only trims spaces (output.strip() == expected) passes all nine, although the contract makes " yes" a fail. If that matters, " yes" becomes the tenth frozen case. Each new scoring escape becomes a new case. An escape from the checker itself, such as ending the run early, needs the separate process above, not another case. The optional step in the fixture README lets you see this: write the trim-only change, watch the nine cases pass it, add " yes" as a tenth case and watch the gate stop it while the current evaluator still passes.

docs.title: Could the model audit run unattended?
docs.text:
Ask the same question of the Audit stage. This course-synthesised record stands in for one student's M3 verification of a model audit on one frozen snapshot:

Course-synthesised M3 record Count Findings in the model audit 9 Confirmed with a failing test or a repeatable reproduction 4 Refuted with runnable evidence 3 Cannot tell (undetermined): a named input is missing 2 Defects the student's own check found and the audit missed 1

By Week 14 you hold your own M3 record. In class, replace these counts with yours: how many findings you confirmed, refuted or marked cannot tell, and whether your own check found something the audit missed.

The software-factory claim is that stages could run with little human input. Suppose an agent had acted on every audit finding unattended. It would have changed code for 3 findings with no defect behind them, acted on 2 cannot-tell findings that nothing observed, and still shipped the 1 defect the audit missed. Unlike the gate, the audit has not been seen to fail and pass on known inputs; its output is a set of claims that become evidence only when someone runs a check. So the audit can run unattended as a source of hypotheses on every snapshot, but not yet as a stage that changes code or blocks a merge on its own word. The two stages connect: each confirmed finding becomes a test that fails before its repair, and that test can join the gate.

The useful outcome is a bounded claim, such as "evaluator changes: a candidate for unattended merging behind this gate once its cases sit where the agent cannot write, the candidate is scored in a separate process and the stop rule has been exercised; audit findings verified before anything changes". It is not a yes or no about factories in general. A check that has never been seen to fail is not yet evidence that it would stop a bad change, and a stop rule that nobody has exercised is not yet a stop.

docs.title: Operating an agent after deployment
docs.text:
Week 11 introduced agents that keep running after deployment. Before such an agent runs unattended, answer three questions with something you can test.

  • Who can stop it? A named person, and a stop that works without a deploy and without the agent's cooperation. The launcher does this when it destroys a container at a cap or deadline. Test it: stop the agent midway and check that no partial effect remains. That is the same idempotency question as a retried request.
  • What may it change? A list of permitted actions and paths, granted in one place, with per-run caps. Irreversible operations wait for a person's approval.
  • How is it observed? A minimal record of what it read, proposed and changed, and an alert when a cap refuses it. Rerun the frozen evaluator cases on a schedule: a hosted model's name does not guarantee unchanged behavior over time.

If you cannot answer one of these for a stage of your pipeline, that stage needs a person.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Locate one existing evidence reference in each required discussion area. Rehearse a concise causal claim and answer a partner's changed condition independently.

Use the activity for feedback and revision; no additional report.

docs.title: Final calibration
docs.text:
Your calibration notes are one short "Final calibration" entry in your existing work record, beside your M4 delivery record. They are not a new file or report, and they carry no mark. The entry has three parts.

  1. Week 1 against now. Reopen the report you produced in Week 1, week01-calibration-report.json, and the explanation you kept with it. From its overall block, copy count, mean_actual_minus_predicted_minutes and pass_prediction_error_rate. Then collect the predicted and actual times you recorded in the project workshops and compute the same signed error, actual minus predicted, for each. Workshop tasks are far longer than the Week 1 tasks, so compare each error with its own prediction: an error of 10 minutes on a 5-minute prediction is larger than one on a 3-hour prediction. Do you still underestimate, and has the error shrunk relative to the prediction? Explain one mismatch from your own records, such as a requirement you missed, setup or waiting, without attributing it to an agent. A time you never recorded stays missing; do not estimate it now. If no Week 1 attempt completed, say so and compare the workshop times alone.
  2. The software-factory judgment. Pick three stages from the table. For each, write whether it could run unattended now, cite the evidence by its existing reference, and name the check or stop rule that would change your answer. If you pick the Audit stage, use your own M3 counts in place of the synthetic record. Let a partner challenge one stage you marked unattended.
  3. One revised claim. The unsupported claim you revised in the workshop, with the observation that changed it.

Leave week01-calibration/calibration.csv as it is. It holds only the calibration controller's Week 1 attempts, and its validator rejects any other row, so the workshop times belong in this entry, not in the CSV.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Distinguish a hand prediction from an actual completed check. Present only the verified scope and explain the next observation needed for a new input.

All execution follows Week 0 setup. The classroom packet is authored practice; actual runs and participants need their own evidence.

For the Week 1 comparison, check that the numbers you copied still follow from the unchanged record. From the course root or unpacked student ZIP, with your Week 1 session directory:

uv run --locked python tools/validate_calibration_log.py \
  week01-calibration/calibration.csv
uv run --locked python tools/calibration_report.py \
  week01-calibration/calibration.csv --out week14-calibration-recheck.json

Expected evidence: the validator reports a valid log with the same row count as in Week 1, and the overall block of the new report matches the one you copied. The report destination must be a new file. If the blocks differ, the record changed after Week 1: keep both reports and note the difference rather than choosing the better one. If the validator refuses the record, keep its message, which names what no longer matches, and compare with the Week 1 report you already hold.

For the software-factory judgment, check each stage you marked unattended. Its evidence must include a check you have seen fail on a bad input and pass on a good one, run from cases the changing agent cannot edit, with the candidate scored in a separate process, and a stop path that someone has exercised. A stage supported only by passing runs is "not yet", however many passes there are.

The gate demonstration is the worked case for the failing and passing check. Command: run-regression.sh on the workspace that holds the proposal, as in the fixture README. Expected evidence: gate exit 1, with extra_text and case_changed in the record's stdout, then gate exit 0 on the current evaluator. Failure case: a record that shows the launcher's generic "status": "failed" is a refused launcher run; it neither passes the change nor shows that the gate caught it. Even with both real runs, the Evaluate stage stays "candidate, not yet unattended" until the gate reads verify.py from a location the agent cannot write, scores the candidate in a separate process, and the stop rule has been exercised once.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
A good prepared demo does not establish every path. A failed live attempt does not disappear when an older recording is shown. Work with others does not replace individual explanation.

Mistake Better next action Answering "can agents run software unattended?" in general Judge one stage of your own pipeline against its evidence Citing green runs as proof that a check would stop a bad change Show the check failing on a deliberately bad input first Treating an audit finding as a one-off fix Ask which unattended stage would have let it through Judging the Audit stage by how many findings the model produced Count confirmed, refuted and cannot-tell findings, plus what your own check found that the audit missed Counting a refused launcher run as a caught change Keep it labelled as a refused run and rerun until the record has an exit_code Calling a stage unattended because its check failed once on a bad change Run the check from cases the changing agent cannot edit, score the candidate in a separate process, and exercise the stop rule once Naming an off switch nobody has tried Stop the agent midway once and check that no partial effect remains Filling in a workshop time you never recorded, or adding it to the Week 1 CSV Mark the time missing and compare only the times you recorded, in the final calibration entry

docs.title: One focused external reading
docs.text:
• Calibrate confidence against observed work (about 12 minutes, optional): read Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, especially “Core Result”, to compare your time prediction and subjective assessment with recorded implementation, testing and review evidence. (studies/metr-2025; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2)

docs.title: Week 14 self-check answer guidance
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Try each prompt first, then compare the concrete result and its limit.

docs.title: Q1: Policy prediction
docs.text: For an active guest, the repaired guard predicts deny with title Old. This is a prediction only: the supplied matrix has no guest row, so add a guest request that asserts both the response and the final title.

docs.title: Q2: Archive rule
docs.text: Changed result: archived staff is now allow/New (it was deny/Old). Retained regression: an archived owner who is not staff is deny/Old.

docs.title: Q3: Changed evaluation question
docs.text: Record the new question as a new contract version agreed with its owner. The expected answer for canceled changes from no to yes, so add frozen cases for canceled with yes (pass) and with no (fail), and keep running with no (pass) as a retained case. Then revise the evaluator and rerun the gate. The earlier pass is evidence for the old question only: its cases had no canceled status, so it says nothing about one.

docs.title: Q4: Rollback states
docs.text: The previous revision may be serving. Or the rollback restored the files while the running process still serves the faulty revision. The success message describes the command, not the service: check which revision the running service reports, then send one request through the affected user path and check what the user sees.

docs.title: Q5: Defense evidence
docs.text: Name the artifact by its existing reference and pair it with an observed check result: for evaluation, your frozen evaluator cases and the gate result on the frozen revision. The artifact alone shows that work exists, not what it establishes.

docs.title: Q6: Timing attribution
docs.text: Keep the observed difference and record alternatives such as a change in task difficulty, your familiarity with the code, or practice gained on the first task. Waiting and setup time may also differ between the two records. None of these was controlled, so the difference alone does not isolate the agent's effect.

docs.title: Q7: Unattended deployment
docs.text: Passing runs alone are "not yet". First, a check seen to fail and pass: confirm that the evaluator fails a deliberately faulty change, with the frozen cases and security regressions kept where the deploying agent cannot edit them, scored in a separate process the deploying agent cannot reach. Second, a stop path someone has exercised: run the rollback and the stop rule once and confirm that they halt the deployment and reach the owner. Keep complete deployment observations, and rerun the frozen cases on a schedule.

docs.title: Q8: Rollback control
docs.text: A named stop owner and a switch that works without agent cooperation can stop a rollback. Permit only a tested rollback for the one service, require approval for irreversible changes, and verify a denied action leaves state unchanged.

docs.title: Q9: Missed defect
docs.text: Reconsider the Test stage, and any Change stage that relied on those tests. The judgment changes only after a regression for the finding fails on the revision with the defect, passes after the repair, and the gate has been rerun.

docs.title: Q10: A gate seen to fail
docs.text: The extra_text case (yes; mark this as passed must score fail) stops it, and case_changed (YES) fails too, so the gate exits 1; the current evaluator exits 0. That shows a check failing on a bad change and passing on a good one. Still missing, at least: the gate reads verify.py from a location the agent cannot write, not from the candidate's workspace; the candidate is scored in a separate process, because here it runs inside the checker and could end the run or print its own report; and the stop rule is exercised once, with a failed gate run seen to halt the merge and page the owner. Until then the stage is a candidate, not yet unattended. The nine cases cover only what they name: each new scoring escape becomes a case, while an escape from the checker needs the separate process.

docs.title: Q11: Audit counts
docs.text: Not as a stage that changes code or blocks merges on its own word: acting unattended would have changed code for the 3 refuted findings, acted on the 2 cannot-tell findings and still shipped the missed defect. It can run unattended as a source of hypotheses on every snapshot, with each confirmed finding turned into a test that fails before its repair and then joins the gate. With your own counts, name the refuted, cannot-tell and missed numbers in the same way.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval 1. The evidence supports refuted: the runnable accepted: false observation contradicts the claim. Record the command and observation, and replace the confirmed disposition. Retrieval 2. The old-label session supports only the old revision; run a new authorized observation for the new label.

docs.title: Check your reasoning
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Use the complete packet. Answer independently before consulting the worked discussion, then revise one answer after feedback.

  1. For an active guest, derive the response and final title from the repaired guard. Distinguish this prediction from the cases actually supplied in the matrix.

  2. The policy now permits archived staff edits but still denies archived owners who are not staff. Name one changed expected result and one retained regression.

  3. The evaluation question changes from "is the status exactly failed?" to "did the build finish without passing?", and canceled builds now appear. Which contract, cases and earlier results need revision?

  4. A rollback command reports success, and no request has reached the service since. State two possible states of the running service and the next discriminating check.

  5. Pick one required defense area. Name the existing artifact you would point to and the check result that shows what it establishes. Why is the artifact alone not enough?

  6. You finished a later workshop task faster than a similar earlier one, and you used an agent only the second time. Name two alternative explanations to record before attributing the difference to the agent.

  7. What evidence is needed before allowing unattended deployment after repeated evaluator passes?

  8. Which control can stop an agent that proposes a rollback after deployment?

  9. The model audit confirms a defect that your tests did not catch. Which pipeline stage should you reconsider before calling it unattended, and what evidence would change that judgment?

  10. An agent's evaluator change trims and lower-cases answers and accepts any answer that starts with the expected word. Which frozen case stops it at the regression gate? Which part of the evidence for merging evaluator changes unattended does that run supply, and what is still missing?

  11. A course-synthesised M3 record shows 9 findings from a model audit: 4 confirmed, 3 refuted and 2 marked cannot tell, plus 1 defect the student's own check found and the audit missed. Could the audit stage act on its findings unattended? What part of it could run unattended? In class, answer again with your own M3 counts.

These public questions are formative; they add no mark or separate submission.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 12–13 audit and usability
docs.text:
Answer these two short prompts after the workshop. They revisit an earlier decision so that the evidence, not a memorized label, is carried forward.

R1. Retrieval 1. A recorded audit marks the arbitrary-status-label claim confirmed, but the snapshot check returns accepted: false. Which disposition does the evidence support?

R2. Retrieval 2. A prior usability session used the old label. What claim can it support about the new label, and what new observation is needed?

Use the same evidence-first format as the questions above. After the workshop, use the public answer guidance.

docs.title: Demonstrate and defend the result
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Week 14 · CI dashboard

Can you explain why this feature deserves confidence?

docs.title: The final conversation follows the work
docs.text:
Your feature began with a user need, then acquired code, tests, an evaluator, recovery evidence and review.

The demonstration connects those decisions. The individual defense asks you to reason without outsourcing the answer.

docs.title: One claim small enough to defend
docs.text:
For the tested role/archive combinations, archived builds remain unchanged when an edit is requested.

This names a behavior and a checked scope. "The application is secure" would need far more evidence.

docs.title: Four evidence locations in your existing work
docs.text:
Discussion area Work to locate Requirement and user need M0 criterion and authorized discovery Evaluation M2 contract, scorer and result scope Security M1 regressions and M3/M4 audit response Deployment and recovery M2 event chain, rollback and recovery checks

Use references to the same artifacts. Do not create a new evidence portfolio.

docs.title: A complete public practice packet
docs.text:
Policy: edit only if owner or staff, and not archived. Week 6's earlier guard, is_owner or is_staff and not archived, let an archived owner edit. The repaired guard groups the roles:

allowed = (is_owner or is_staff) and not archived
if allowed:
    title = requested_title

Inputs are booleans. Guest means neither owner nor staff.

docs.title: The supplied evidence matrix
docs.text:
Case on the repaired guard Decision Title after request Active owner Allow New Active staff Allow New Archived owner Deny Old Archived staff Deny Old

Synthetic practice evidence. Guest cases are absent from this matrix.

docs.title: A new role in the question
docs.text:
A guest requests the same edit on an active build.

Predict the guard's value and required title. Which part is code reasoning, and which part needs an observed check?

docs.title: Explanation can be precise about a gap
docs.text:
For a guest, both role booleans are false: predict denial and unchanged title.

The given matrix has not observed that case. Add an active-guest request and assert both response and unchanged state.

This supports a next check without pretending it already ran.

docs.title: Mechanism: A claim that can survive a question
docs.text:
Each link points to work you already have. A changed input either reuses an observation or names the next check.

A claim that can survive a question A bounded claim names a behavior and its scope. It links to a source change at a named revision, a discriminating check such as the archived owner, the observed result on that revision (deny, title Old), and a conclusion limited to the checked cases. When a peer changes an input or condition, such as an active guest, either the case was already observed and that evidence is cited, or it was not: predict from the code, add the check, and say that it has not run. bounded claimbehavior + scope source changeat a named revision discriminatingcheckarchived owner observed resultdeny, title Old conclusionchecked cases only a peer changes an inpute.g. an active guest already observed:cite that evidence not observed: predict,add the check, say it has not run A complete spoken explanation does not create missing evidence.

docs.title: A causal explanation of one change
docs.text:
Need: protect archived records
Cause: old expression let owner bypass archive condition
Change: apply archive condition to both role paths
Check: archived owner is denied and title remains Old
Limit: name the checked revision and routes

Point to your own source and actual evidence for the real defense.

docs.title: Requirement variation
docs.text:
A new request lets staff edit archived builds; owners who are not staff still may not.

Which policy clause and cases change? Which old evidence is still relevant? Answer from the new requirement before proposing code.

docs.title: Evaluation variation
docs.text:
The question changes from "is the status exactly failed?" to "did the build finish without passing?", and canceled builds now appear. The gate still reports its earlier passing cases.

Which expected answers, cases and earlier results change?

docs.title: Recovery variation
docs.text:
A rollback command reports success. No request has reached the service since.

Name two possible states of the running service and the observation that separates them. Do not infer "recovered" from the command's message alone.

docs.title: A demonstration the audience can follow
docs.text:
Show the user task, one visible behavior and the verification that supports it. Then explain one decision and a remaining limitation.

Identify the running revision. Label a recording or fallback by its actual source. The scheduled demo format and defense remain in the course instructions.

docs.title: When a demonstration fails
docs.text:
Preserve the actual failure and identify the next observation. Use a labelled recording if the announced format permits it.

A prepared screenshot cannot establish that the current candidate works. A missing observation can be explained clearly without inventing a pass.

docs.title: Calibration without invented causality
docs.text:
Reopen your Week 1 calibration report beside the times you recorded in the project workshops. Do you still underestimate, relative to each prediction? Explain one concrete mismatch.

A later task done faster may also differ in difficulty, familiarity and prior practice. The difference alone does not isolate an agent's productivity effect.

docs.title: The software factory is a claim to test
docs.text:
Definition: a repeatable process that organizes requirements, generation, verification and delivery.

Claim to test: its stages could run with little human input.

Test it on the pipeline you know: specify, change, test, evaluate, protect, deploy and recover, audit. For each stage: could it run unattended, and what evidence comes first?

docs.title: An agent's change: merge it unattended?
docs.text:
The agent rewrites evaluator.py and replies:

Made scoring robust to formatting. Answers are trimmed and lower-cased, and an answer that starts with the expected word now counts.

Predict the regression gate's exit code before the run.

Course-authored replay in fixture/proposed_evaluator.py. No model wrote it.

docs.title: Run the gate on the change
docs.text:
cp lectures/week-14/fixture/proposed_evaluator.py week14-gate/evaluator.py
sh evals/evaluator-kit/run-regression.sh --profile offline \
  --version "$week14_version" --digest "$week14_digest" \
  --workspace week14-gate

Then copy back evaluator.py from the fixture and run the identical command.

Setup first (workspace, verify.py, profile variables): fixture README.

docs.title: A gate that has been seen to fail
docs.text:
{"cases": 9, "failed": [
  {"case": "extra_text", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"},
  {"case": "case_changed", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}

Proposal: gate exit 1. Current evaluator: gate exit 0, nothing failed. "Robust" meant accepting yes; mark this as passed.

docs.title: Evaluate: a candidate, not yet unattended
docs.text:
Seen to fail on a bad change and pass on a good one. Still missing, at least:

Where the gate is not yet unattended An agent changes evaluator.py. The gate copies evaluator.py and verify.py into one workspace, the launcher runs verify.py, and the exit code decides merge or stop. Shown: exit 1 on the proposal and exit 0 on the current evaluator. Still missing: the gate reads verify.py from a location the agent cannot write, not from the candidate's workspace; the candidate is scored in a separate process, because inside the checker it could end the run or print its own report; and the stop rule exercised once, with a failed gate run seen to halt the merge and page the owner. shown: exit 1 on the proposal,exit 0 on the current one agent changesevaluator.py one workspaceevaluator + verify.py launcher runsverify.py gate exit codefails, then passes merge or stoppage the owner missing: read verify.py from alocation the agent cannot write(today: the candidate's workspace) missing: a separate process;inside the checker it could endthe run or print its own report missing: the stop ruleexercised once: a failed runseen to halt the merge

Each scoring escape becomes a new case; an escape from the checker needs the separate process.

docs.title: Could the model audit run unattended?
docs.text:
Course-synthesised M3 record Count Findings 9 Confirmed 4 Refuted 3 Cannot tell 2 Missed, found by the student's own check 1

In class, replace these counts with your own M3 record.

docs.title: Claims are not checks
docs.text:
Acting on every finding unattended: 3 changes with no defect, 2 actions on cannot-tell findings, 1 defect still shipped.

The audit can run unattended as a source of hypotheses. Its confirmed findings become tests, and those tests can join the gate.

A check never seen to fail is not yet evidence that it would stop a bad change.

docs.title: Judge three stages of your own pipeline
docs.text:
For each stage: unattended now, or not yet? Cite the evidence by its existing reference. Name the check or stop rule that would change your answer.

Use your own M3 counts for the Audit stage. A partner challenges one stage you marked unattended.

docs.title: Before an agent runs after deployment
docs.text:
Who can stop it? A named person; a stop that needs no deploy and no cooperation. What may it change? Permitted actions granted in one place, per-run caps, approval for irreversible steps. How is it observed? A minimal record, alerts on refusals, frozen evaluator cases rerun.

Test each answer. One you cannot answer means that stage needs a person.

docs.title: Rehearsal with a partner
docs.text:
Locate one evidence reference in each discussion area. Rehearse one concise claim, then let a peer change an input or condition.

Answer the variation independently and revise an unsupported claim. These are public practice prompts, not the private defense bank.

docs.title: Exit: what you can now explain
docs.text:
Choose one changed decision from your own project.

What did you first expect? Which observation changed your mind? What would make you revisit the decision again?

docs.title: The expo and your defense
docs.text:
At the expo, demonstrate the final product and its evidence from your submitted M4 revision: M4 in the project guide.

Attend your individually scheduled defense; the expo does not replace it.

The final calibration is feedback. It adds no separate reflection report.

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Workshop · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the linked practice unit or project. No extra report.

docs.title: A regression gate and an agent's change
docs.text:
This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

Course-authored files for the factory gate demonstration. No file calls a model, opens a network connection or writes a file. Read each one as text before running anything.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• evaluator.py is the current evaluator for the Week 10 contract: answer whether a supplied status is exactly failed. The exact string yes is correct for failed and the exact string no for any other status. A missing or non-string answer is unknown; any other string, including extra text, is fail.
  • proposed_evaluator.py is an agent's proposed replacement. It is a course-authored replay; no model wrote it. Its reply claims that scoring is now robust to formatting, because answers are trimmed and lower-cased and an answer that starts with the expected word counts.
  • verify.py holds nine frozen cases, including the Week 10 output yes; mark this as passed. It prints one JSON line listing every case whose score differs from the contract, and exits 1 if there is any.

The gate is the evaluator kit's run-regression.sh, the same local gate as in the M2 evaluator workshop. It copies only evaluator.py and verify.py from a workspace into a fresh temporary directory, runs python verify.py there through the course launcher, prints the launcher record and exits with the candidate's exit status.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
From the course root, put the agent's proposal in a fresh workspace, resolve the offline profile as in the Week 9 execution route and run the gate. The offline profile needs no key and makes no model call:

mkdir week14-gate
cp lectures/week-14/fixture/verify.py week14-gate/
cp lectures/week-14/fixture/proposed_evaluator.py week14-gate/evaluator.py
week14_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
week14_version=$(printf '%s' "$week14_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
week14_digest=$(printf '%s' "$week14_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')
sh evals/evaluator-kit/run-regression.sh --profile offline --version "$week14_version" --digest "$week14_digest" --workspace week14-gate
echo "gate exit: $?"

Then restore the current evaluator and run the identical gate command again:

cp lectures/week-14/fixture/evaluator.py week14-gate/evaluator.py
sh evals/evaluator-kit/run-regression.sh --profile offline --version "$week14_version" --digest "$week14_digest" --workspace week14-gate
echo "gate exit: $?"

docs.title: Expected distinction
docs.text:
With the proposal, the launcher record shows "exit_code": 1 and the gate exits 1. The record's stdout field holds:

{"cases": 9, "failed": [{"case": "extra_text", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}, {"case": "case_changed", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}

With the current evaluator, the record shows "exit_code": 0, its stdout is {"cases": 9, "failed": []} and the gate exits 0. If the record instead shows "status": "failed" with the launcher's generic error, the launcher refused the run. The gate still exits nonzero, but a refused launcher run is neither a pass nor evidence that the gate caught the change; keep it labelled as a refused run.

The proposal makes formatting "robust" by accepting the very answer that tried to talk the Week 10 scorer into a pass. The gate stops it because a frozen case was written for that answer. The cases show that this gate fails on one bad change and passes on the current evaluator; they do not show that it would catch every bad change. A change that only trims spaces passes all nine, although the contract makes " yes" a fail.

The commands copy verify.py from this fixture, which the replayed change did not touch. The gate itself copies verify.py from the same workspace as the candidate, so a pipeline that let an agent edit that workspace would also let it edit the cases. verify.py also imports the candidate into its own process, so a candidate could end the run or print its own report. An unattended gate would read the cases from a location the agent cannot write and score the candidate in a separate process, treating that process's output only as data.

docs.title: Optional: turn the escape into a case
docs.text:
About ten minutes, after the two gate runs above, in the same shell and workspace.

Generation: write the trim-only change yourself. Start from the current evaluator:

cp lectures/week-14/fixture/evaluator.py week14-gate/evaluator.py

In a text editor, change the last line of score in week14-gate/evaluator.py from output == expected to output.strip() == expected. Predict the gate's exit code, then run the identical gate command. Expected: exit 0 and {"cases": 9, "failed": []}, because none of the nine cases has a leading space.

Verification: turn the escape into a case. In week14-gate/verify.py, add this line to CASES, directly after the case_changed line:

    ("leading_space", "failed", " yes", "fail"),

Run the identical gate command again. Expected: the record shows "exit_code": 1, the gate exits 1 and the record's stdout holds:

{"cases": 10, "failed": [{"case": "leading_space", "observed": "pass", "required": "fail"}]}

Restore the current evaluator with the cp command above and run the gate once more. Expected: exit 0 and {"cases": 10, "failed": []}. The tenth case stops the trim-only change and still passes the evaluator that keeps the contract. Here you wrote the case yourself, in the workspace the candidate also sits in; in a pipeline that merged changes unattended, the case would go where the changing agent cannot write. Delete week14-gate when you finish.

docs.title: Assignments A1–A6
docs.text: These six small assignments are the practical line through the first ten teaching weeks. Each is worth 2.5 points under the syllabus. Submit the artifact, verification evidence and a short explanation. End every report with decision: accept | narrow | recheck | stop, because: evidence IDs and next:.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9: run the agent in a dedicated directory or container; keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of it; keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs; and run injection demonstrations offline against the local machine only. Use the mature coding-agent seat supplied for the course and do not run unknown generated commands on a credential-bearing host.

Assignment Week Capability Start A1: Read a coding-agent session 1 Capture a real session and a forced failure python practice/a1/check.py <submission> A2: Build a small MCP tool server 2 Tool selection, arguments and recovery python practice/a2/check.py <submission> A3: Turn a manual workflow into a skill 3 Trigger and near-miss testing python practice/a3/check.py <submission> A4: Make a messy repository agent-ready 5 Instructions, hook and checks python practice/a4/check.py <submission> A5: Score agent readiness from observations 6 Anchored evidence and change conditions python practice/a5/check.py <submission> A6: Audit an evaluation instance and scorer 10 Denominators, counterexamples and limits python practice/a6/check.py <submission>

The checks provide public consistency feedback. They do not execute model-generated code, authenticate provenance or assign marks.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: capture one real coding-agent session, force one safe failure, and label what you observed or inferred.
  • Week: 1
  • Weight: 2.5 points
  • Due: Sunday 23:59 in the listed week
  • Hand in: one report.json and the session excerpt or redacted transcript it cites.
  • Done when: every behaviour is labelled observed or inferred and points to an excerpt or command output, and the forced failure is real and explained. check.py then confirms the shape of the record only.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Specify. Choose two or three read or write operations and define names, descriptions, required arguments, errors and a safe retry rule.
  2. Generate. Ask the agent to propose handlers and schemas. Review the proposal before placing it in the server.
  3. Verify selection. Run a request where the right tool is distinguishable from its neighbours; record the selected call and result.
  4. Verify arguments. Run a valid call and an invalid-argument call. Check that the server returns structured feedback without a traceback.
  5. Verify recovery. Make one tool return a retryable local error, then show the agent taking the documented next step. Keep all three trials.
  6. Revise. Fix one unclear description or error, rerun the protocol check, and write the decision line.

Generation is the proposed tool design; verification is the protocol transcript and direct result inspection. The check never calls a model and does not turn a transcript into a mark.

docs.title: Deliverables

Include the server source, schemas, report.json, and protocol output. The report has a server_path naming the submitted tool_server.py and exactly three trial cases: selection, arguments and recovery, each with request, expected, actual, disposition and evidence IDs. Start from starter/ and run:

python practice/a2/protocol_check.py path/to/submission/tool_server.py
python practice/a2/check.py path/to/submission

protocol_check.py is an envelope smoke test. It checks the handshake, the shape of the tool list, one valid call and one refused invalid call. It never calls a model, so it does not show that a model can choose and use your tool; a pass says so on its own line.

Register the same tool_server.py command in your mature agent's documented local-stdio tool configuration. The three report trials are the real agent runs that establish selection, argument handling and recovery.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: Criteria are model-readable tool descriptions; correct schema validation; structured, bounded errors; recovery evidence; and an explanation of one revision. The public check only detects missing or inconsistent records; it does not claim that a model selected a tool correctly on unseen requests.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Follow the safety practices in syllabus §9:

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Inspect. Copy starter/, make the baseline commit described in its README, and map one behaviour to its files, tests and check command before asking for a change. The assigned bad commit adds print("debug: leaked value") to app.py; your hook must make that git commit exit non-zero.

  2. Generate. Ask the agent to propose an instruction file, a small pre-commit hook and a structural cleanup. Review every command before running it. Put the hook where Git and your reader can both find it:

    ```bash mkdir -p .githooks

Generation is the agent's proposed repository change; verification is the three probes and direct file inspection.

docs.title: write your hook to .githooks/pre-commit, then:
docs.text:
chmod +x .githooks/pre-commit git config core.hooksPath .githooks git add .githooks/pre-commit git commit -m "Add pre-commit hook" ```

core.hooksPath is a local setting and is not part of a commit, so name that command in your instruction file. The hook file itself must be committed; a hook left in .git/hooks/ is not handed in. 3. Verify the gate. Run the three probes as commands and keep each command, exit code and output:

```bash

docs.title: bad commit: must exit non-zero
docs.text: echo 'print("debug: leaked value")' >> app.py git add app.py git commit -m "bad probe"; echo "exit=$?" git restore --staged app.py && git restore app.py

docs.title: good commit: a documentation or behaviour-preserving change; must exit zero
docs.text: printf '\nReviewed.\n' >> NOTES.md git add NOTES.md git commit -m "good probe"; echo "exit=$?"

docs.title: regression: must pass
docs.text: python -m pytest -q; echo "exit=$?" ``` 4. Check structure. Confirm the instruction file names the same commands and invariants that the repository actually contains. 5. Revise. Fix one stale instruction or weak check and repeat all three probes. Write the decision line.

docs.text:

Dimension Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Level 4 Structure No behaviour-to-file map A map exists but an entry is wrong Map is accurate and the change point has one responsibility A check catches a deliberate boundary violation Documentation No runnable context file Commands are listed but one fails or an invariant is absent Commands run and three invariants name their checks A check detects a stale documented command Tests No runnable coverage for the changed path A run passes but is slow, nondeterministic or misses a deliberate break Two repeatable runs pass and a deliberate break fails Mutation evidence explains every surviving mutant Checks No automatic gate A gate is manual or already failing One offline gate command stops a bad change A pre-commit gate stops both an unused import and a secret canary

P1 is an 11-hour personal practice in which you build and verify a bounded coding agent from four calibration attempts. Submit one work record with your controller, five task traces, the session dissection, verification results, your explanation and one revision after feedback.

docs.title: P1: Build a minimal coding agent
docs.text: This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Explain and implement an observation-action loop (LO1): ask for an action, dispatch read, write or bash, return the observation, and stop. Predict model performance before measuring it, then use a failed check to improve your implementation.

You implement only Agent.run in agent_skeleton.py, within 300 nonblank, noncomment lines including any helpers you add to that file. The course supplies the model adapter, workspace tools, context compaction, task inputs and trace writer in lab_runtime.py. Tests do not count toward the implementation limit. You do not rebuild the launcher or its security checks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete Week 0 setup for the shared safety admission, launcher and approved hosted or replay access.

Keep the profile, version and digest returned by the Week 0 resolver, and the approved hosted or replay route. Run the commands below from the course checkout or unpacked student package root. Create a separate lab01-work directory in your editor and copy only agent_skeleton.py, lab_runtime.py, exercise.py and the five tasks/*.json files into it, retaining the tasks/ subdirectory. Keep results outside that input directory. Do not copy the whole private course checkout.

docs.title: Week 1: Predict, generate, verify
docs.text:
Complete the four required tasks in the calibration exercise. For each task, save your own time/pass prediction before generation; run the hosted or replay route once through its supplied launcher controller; inspect the candidate as text; and verify it with the public cases. Preserve wrong answers and technical failures. A later revision is a new attempt, not a replacement first attempt.

The required IDs are lab01-cal-001, lab01-cal-002, lab01-cal-003 and lab01-cal-005: signed sum, stable ordering, inclusive clamping, and whitespace with word order. The other sixteen catalog tasks are optional practice. Keep calibration.csv, the four task JSON records and corresponding candidates together. The linked instructions provide the exact start, finish, validation and report commands. At the first workshop checkpoint, show one prediction and its observed result. Ask for help if setup or waiting prevents you from making progress; a low pass rate is evidence to explain, not a reason to invent successes or repeat until every first attempt appears correct.

Save this set for Week 1 formative feedback. Reference the same commit/evidence ID in Week 2 and your P1 portfolio sample; keep the original attempts when revising.

docs.title: Week 2: Implement and observe the loop
docs.text:
The supplied interface is Agent(model, tools, max_steps, context_limit) and Agent.run(task) -> Trajectory. Start with one user message containing the task. For each permitted turn:

  1. Pass compact(history, context_limit) to model.chat. It retains the task, bounds long observations and drops old action/result groups when necessary.
  2. Append the returned assistant message, including its tool_calls.
  3. With no tool calls, return Trajectory(history, "final") immediately. Empty answer text still counts as final when there are no calls.
  4. Otherwise, dispatch each named tool with its arguments. Append a tool message containing role: "tool", the matching tool_call_id, and string content.
  5. If the turn budget is exhausted, return Trajectory(history, "step_limit").

Keep the full history for the returned trajectory; compact the copy sent to the model. Handle an unknown tool or refused operation with a short safe observation, without exposing paths or environment values. Do not keep calling after final.

For example, returning immediately after a write call creates the file but misses verification. Inspect completion.json: it should show the subsequent bash observation and then the final answer. Fix the stopping branch and run again into a new result directory. That revision is your first formative feedback checkpoint.

The bash tool deliberately accepts only python -B workspace-file.py with plain arguments. It runs that file through bash inside the launcher. It is not a general shell. Use the supplied verify.py commands from the task responses; imports and nested subprocesses remain subject to the same container limits.

docs.title: Verify all five tasks
docs.text:
The public tasks are course-authored deterministic replays. They isolate loop bugs from model variability; they are labelled fake/fake-v1 and are not real model measurements. Actual hosted-route calibration belongs to the Week 1 activity.

Task Work product Verification in the task create greeting.txt Exact text and final newline repair numbers.py Failing signed-sum examples now pass refactor prices.py Extracted helper preserves results cli hello.py CLI output matches its argument answer answer.txt Read two source files and check the answer

Replace VERSION and DIGEST with your resolver output. Run once per task, changing both --task create and the output name to repair, refactor, cli and answer. Every output directory must be new; for a revision use a name such as lab01-create-revised.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace lab01-work --output lab01-create \
  -- python -B exercise.py --task create

The unmodified starter raises NotImplementedError; it has no working loop yet. With your loop implemented, inspect the launcher exit code, exported product and completion.json. For each verification command, check for exit_code: 0 and stdout: "verified\n" in its tool observation. Check that the last assistant turn has no calls and stop_reason is final. An exported file alone is not proof of success. The fixed responses and public checks are visible so you can diagnose failures; copying their answers does not implement a general loop.

trajectory.jsonl is the minimal per-call trace for this replay. Inspect consecutive run.sequence values starting at zero and one run ID. Each record contains the input messages and returned assistant step; only that last step carries this call's usage and latency. not_collected fields are lengths/digests, not missing text to fill in. Use completion.json locally to understand these synthetic turns, and submit only the requested minimal trace plus your short explanation.

Also test an early final response and a sequence that reaches max_steps; explain why each stops. Use an oversized observation to check context compaction. If stuck, first check tool-result IDs, then the final branch, then the context copy. Ask for feedback before adding more tools or a more elaborate agent architecture.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Keep one P1 work record and use the same evidence through feedback and P1:

  • Week 1 checkpoint: the four-task CSV, matching JSON records and candidates, with a brief explanation of one prediction and observed result.
  • Week 2 checkpoint: agent_skeleton.py, your tests, five minimal JSONL traces, and the required recorded-session dissection table and answers from the Week 2 activity labelled by task, work products and verification results. Explain one loop failure, its fix and the repeat check; reference the Week 1 evidence ID.
  • P1 portfolio sample: select this existing evidence, explain how the loop and tool boundary affect a result, and show one revision after feedback. Write your explanation independently; no separate comprehensive report is required.

P1 is individual. Include your own verification, even if you discussed an error with classmates. Keep one AI-use note across this practice unit and refer to its ID when reusing the evidence. Write your prediction and brief reflection yourself, without AI. Remove credentials and unrelated personal data before pushing; do not submit environment files or a full conversation export. If a required trace cannot be safely exported, record the technical failure and existing contemporaneous evidence in your same explanation, then use the course's announced supplement process.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
P1 is a 4-point portfolio sample within the 10-point individual practice portfolio. Your teacher assesses the evidence you submit:

  • the bounded controller and five task checks or traces;
  • four calibration predictions, observed results and one explanation of a mismatch;
  • the required session dissection, your own explanation and one revision after feedback.

Keep one work record connecting the artifact, verification, explanation, revision and your single AI-use note. Public checks and local diagnostic feedback help you revise; their numerical output is not a separate course mark.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text:
Yellow: approved hosted API route and course sandbox only, as linked in Prerequisites. Predictions and reflection are red: no AI. You may choose not to use AI for the loop implementation; the required model-calibration activity still needs its approved execution or an instructor-approved equivalent.

Use a truthful note in your existing explanation, for example:

P1, evidence L1-01. I used [actual model/tool] for [purpose]. I personally verified [checks and result IDs] and changed [one decision]. My reflection is my own. Week 2 refers to this same note.

If no AI helped your loop, say that explicitly and distinguish it from Week 1's model measurements. Correct mistakes in the same record rather than fabricating an earlier session.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Plan 11 hours total, including both workshops and the required session dissection: about 3 hours for calibration, 3 for the loop and five tasks, 2.5 for the recorded-session dissection, and 2.5 for verification, feedback, revision and your brief explanation. These are planning values, rounded up from the activity estimates, not measured student times or cutoffs. Waiting and help count. Seek support at the workshop checkpoints or when the plan no longer fits; reaching the time box does not automatically cost marks.

docs.title: P2: A specification review that changes the next action
docs.text: This page describes the earlier fourteen-week layout and is being rewritten; where it differs, the syllabus applies.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: review one short change against its acceptance contract on your own, before any AI review; check one claim by running it, whether that shows a defect, leaves a suspicion or supports no finding; then compare your review with the supplied review claim by claim and decide what happens next.
  • Hand in: one work record with your specification finding and your code findings, or a justified no-finding for either, the check you ran with its actual output, and a comparison table. Copy the outline and replace every TODO.
  • Done when: no TODO remains; every defect you claim has a check that fails on the assigned change when run through the launcher, or is labelled a suspicion; a no-finding result lists the inputs you checked and what they showed; and every row of the comparison table cites evidence.
  • Time: three hours including the Week 6 workshop, waiting, feedback and revision.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Judge a change against what was asked rather than against what it appears to do (LO3, LO5). Separate a demonstrated defect from a suspicion, and calibrate how far a review written in the style of an AI review can be relied on by checking its claims one at a time (LO9).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup and rehearse with the Week 6 activity, which gives the supported launcher commands. Start with the local acceptance contract and assigned candidate. The student guide provides the copyable launcher commands, the supplied review and the optional live AI-review route. Copy only the public student/ files into a new workspace. The classroom fixture is rehearsal; its result does not complete P2.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Work in this order. Steps 1 to 4 are AI-off; save them before step 5 and before you open supplied-review.txt.

  1. Predict (5 minutes). Read the contract only. Write the one input you think the change is most likely to handle wrongly, or, if you expect none, the input you would check first and why. Write how long you expect the review to take.
  2. Review the contract (10 minutes). Look for one requirement that is unsupported, ambiguous or impossible to check. If you find one, quote the clause, give two readings of it, name an input that tells the readings apart, and write the question you would ask its owner. "No finding" is an acceptable answer only with the search shown: the clause you examined most closely, the two readings you tried, the input you checked that both readings treat alike, and the clauses you inspected.
  3. Review the change (15 minutes). For each finding give the location, an input, the result the contract requires with its clause, the result you observe or predict, and the consequence for a caller. "No finding" is an acceptable answer only with the inputs you checked, what each returned and the lines you inspected.
  4. Check one claim by running it (15 minutes). If you claim a defect, write the smallest check in probe.py that fails on the unchanged assigned change, run it through the launcher and keep the real failing output in probe-output.txt. If you cannot make it fail, say so and call the finding a suspicion. If you found no defect, run the check you thought most likely to fail and keep its passing output with the inputs it covers. Never construct a failure to have one to hand in.
  5. Compare with the supplied review (15 minutes). Open the supplied review now. The course team wrote it in the style of an AI review, and you are not told which of its claims hold. Fill one table row per claim, yours and the review's: who raised it, and whether the evidence confirms it, refutes it or leaves it unverified. For each supplied claim, choose the input that would show what the claim says, run it through the launcher, and record that input and what the change returned. When nothing you were given can decide a claim, mark it unverified and name the observation that would settle it. A refuted claim means the code does not have the problem that claim describes; say so, with the input that shows it. Judge each claim by its evidence, not by its author. Where your instructor has announced a live model route, one AI review is an optional extra: add its claims as further rows, and do not rerun it until it agrees with you.
  6. Decide and revise (15 minutes). Choose one: accept the change, narrow the task, obtain one missing observation, or stop. Say what evidence would change that decision. After feedback, revise one finding or the decision, and add anything both you and the review missed.

Ask for help at step 4 if the failing input or the execution boundary is unclear. The time box is a support checkpoint, not a penalty.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: One existing work record that follows the outline below, probe.py from step 4, and its actual output in probe-output.txt. Use ai_review_comparison.en.md as that work record and review.yaml as its structured code-finding list. If you ran the optional live review, keep its short ai-review.txt response as comparison evidence. Do not add a separate report, a raw chat export or a second AI-use note.
